# tensordict

> A dict[str, torch.Tensor] that behaves like one tensor.


---

# Which container should I use?

Most code needs one of two forms of the same container. Use a
[`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict), the dict form, when your program chooses the
keys at run time. Use a [`TensorClass`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass), the class form, when
you know the fields in advance and want methods on them. Both forms have the
same tensor operations, and `from_tensordict` wraps the dict form in the
class form without a copy:

```
>>> import torch
>>> from tensordict import TensorClass, TensorDict
>>> td = TensorDict({"pos": torch.zeros(4, 3), "vel": torch.zeros(4, 3)}, batch_size=[4])
>>> td["mass"] = torch.ones(4) # add a key at run time
>>> class Particles(TensorClass):
... pos: torch.Tensor
... vel: torch.Tensor
... mass: torch.Tensor
>>> particles = Particles.from_tensordict(td) # wraps td
>>> particles.pos += 1 # writes to td
>>> td["pos"][0]
tensor([1., 1., 1.])
```

`from_tensordict` raises `ValueError` if the tensordict has a key that is
not a field. `to_tensordict()` returns the data in the dict form, as a copy.

The other containers are special cases: items of different shapes, data on
disk or on a server, and typed fields on a `TensorDictBase`. All the
containers except the plain `dict` have a *batch size*: the leading
dimensions that all their entries share (see [Batch size, shapes, and indexing](concepts/batch_size.html#batch-size)). Indexing,
reshaping, and stacking apply to these dimensions.

## The containers

| Container | Use it for | Main constraint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict) | Tensors that share their batch dimensions, under string keys or nested keys that you add and remove at any time. The data is in memory, on any device. | Each entry must start with the batch dimensions. Any other value raises `RuntimeError: batch dimension mismatch`. |
| [`TensorClass`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass) | A fixed set of fields that you declare like a dataclass, with attribute access, your own methods, and plain Python values for fields that are not tensors. | It is not a [`TensorDictBase`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase) or a `Mapping`: `tc["key"]` and `**tc` raise `ValueError`, and a function that tests `isinstance(x, TensorDictBase)` rejects it. |
| [`LazyStackedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict.html#tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict) | A stack of tensordicts whose entries have different shapes, for example sequences of different lengths. [`lazy_stack()`](reference/generated/tensordict.lazy_stack.html#tensordict.lazy_stack) makes one. It keeps the stacked tensordicts, so a write to the stack changes them. | Each read of an entry stacks it into a new tensor. An entry with different shapes raises `RuntimeError` unless you ask for a padded tensor, a nested tensor, or a list (`get(key, as_padded_tensor=True)`). `keys()` lists only the keys that all the stacked tensordicts have. |
| [`PersistentTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.html#tensordict.PersistentTensorDict) | Data in an HDF5 or Zarr file, read on demand. The file can be larger than the memory. | Each read loads a new tensor from the file, so an in-place operation on that tensor does not change the file. The in-place methods of the tensordict, such as `add_()` and `update_()`, write to the file when it is open for writing (`mode="r+"`); `from_h5()` and `from_zarr()` open it read-only by default. Needs `h5py` or `zarr`. |
| [`TensorDictStore`](reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore) | Data on a Redis, Dragonfly, or KeyDB server, which several processes or machines can read and write. | Needs a running server and the `redis` package. Each read goes over the network. The data stays on the server until you call `clear_redis()`. |
| [`TypedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TypedTensorDict.html#tensordict.TypedTensorDict) | Declared fields on a class that is a `TensorDictBase`, with `**state` unpacking and the full tensordict API. | Experimental: its API can change in a minor release without a deprecation cycle (see [TypedTensorDict](typed_tensordict.html#typed-tensordict-guide)). Attribute access returns a string field as a [`NonTensorData`](reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData) wrapper. No custom `__init__` and no `__post_init__`. |
| A plain `dict` of tensors | Any Python values, with no rule on their shapes. | No batch dimensions: you write a loop, or a `torch.utils._pytree.tree_map` call, for each operation on the values. |

On `PersistentTensorDict` and `TensorDictStore`, use `set_()` for each
key, or `update(d, inplace=True)`, instead of `update_()`.
[Containers on storage backends](compatibility.html#compatibility) lists this limit with the other limits of each backend.

## Choose by need

- If your program chooses the keys at run time, use a
[`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict). See [What is TensorDict?](overview.html#overview).
- If you know the fields and want methods of your own and completion in your
editor, use a [`TensorClass`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass). See [TensorClass](tensorclass.html#tensorclass-guide).
- If you want declared fields on an object that is a `TensorDictBase`, use
a [`TypedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TypedTensorDict.html#tensordict.TypedTensorDict). It accepts `state["key"]` and
`**state`, and a function that takes a tensordict accepts it. See
[TypedTensorDict](typed_tensordict.html#typed-tensordict-guide).
- If you stack items of different shapes, use
[`lazy_stack()`](reference/generated/tensordict.lazy_stack.html#tensordict.lazy_stack), which returns a
[`LazyStackedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict.html#tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict). See [Stacking and variable-size data](concepts/stacking.html#stacking).
- If your dataset is larger than the memory and is on a local disk, save a
`TensorDict` with [`memmap_()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap_) and load it with
[`load_memmap()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap). Its entries are then
memory-mapped tensors. See [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving).
- If your data is in HDF5 or Zarr files, use a
[`PersistentTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.html#tensordict.PersistentTensorDict). See [Large datasets and storage backends](storage.html#storage).
- If several processes or machines must share the data through a server, use
a [`TensorDictStore`](reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore). See [Large datasets and storage backends](storage.html#storage).
- If you want typed fields on a file, a server, or a lazy stack, wrap it with
`from_tensordict` of a `TensorClass` or a `TypedTensorDict`. See
[Containers on storage backends](compatibility.html#compatibility).
- If your values have no common leading dimension, use a plain `dict`, or
put them in a tensordict with `batch_size=[]`.

## TensorClass or TypedTensorDict?

`TypedTensorDict` is experimental: its API can change in a minor release
without a deprecation cycle (see [TypedTensorDict](typed_tensordict.html#typed-tensordict-guide)).
`TensorClass` follows the normal deprecation rules.

Both declare typed fields with class annotations, and both can wrap a
tensordict of any backend. A [`TensorClass`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass) holds a
tensordict, and a [`TypedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TypedTensorDict.html#tensordict.TypedTensorDict) is one. The other
differences follow from this:

| Feature | `TensorClass` | `TypedTensorDict` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Declaration | `class Foo(TensorClass)`, or the legacy `@tensorclass` decorator | `class Foo(TypedTensorDict)` |
| `isinstance(obj, TensorDictBase)` | `False`. To accept both, use [`is_tensor_collection()`](reference/generated/tensordict.is_tensor_collection.html#tensordict.is_tensor_collection). | `True` |
| `obj["key"]` | Raises `ValueError`. Use `obj.key` or `obj.get("key")`. | Returns the entry. |
| `**obj` | Raises `ValueError`. Use `**obj.to_dict()`, which also turns nested tensorclasses into dicts. | Works: a `TypedTensorDict` is a `MutableMapping`. |
| A `str` field | Attribute access returns the `str`. | Attribute access returns a `NonTensorData` wrapper. `obj["key"]` returns the `str`. |
| A Python number | Becomes a tensor, unless the class has the `nocast` flag. | Becomes a tensor. |
| Optional fields | `x: Tensor \| None = None`. A field that is not set is not in `keys()`. | The same as for `TensorClass`. |
| Class options | `autocast`, `nocast`, `tensor_only`, `frozen`, `shadow` | `shadow` and `frozen`. The other three have no effect, and are deprecated. |
| `frozen` | Attribute assignment raises `dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError`. | Locks the tensordict: attribute assignment raises `RuntimeError`. |
| Methods and properties | Supported | Supported |
| Custom `__init__`, `__post_init__` | Supported | Not supported |
| Wrap another backend | `Foo.from_tensordict(td)`. Writes go to `td`. | The same as for `TensorClass`. |
| Wrap the other class | `Foo.from_tensordict(ttd)` works. | `Foo.from_tensordict(tc)` reads the fields, but an attribute write raises `ValueError`. |
| Type checkers (pyright, mypy) | Report a field value of the wrong type, a missing field, and an unknown keyword argument in the constructor. | Type the fields. Only mypy reports a missing field. Neither reports an unknown keyword argument. |

Use `TensorClass` if:

- Your fields include strings or other Python objects that you read as plain
values.
- You need a custom `__init__`, `__post_init__`, or the `autocast` flag.

Use `TypedTensorDict` if:

- The object must be a `TensorDictBase`.
- Your pipeline builds its state in stages and passes it on with
`**state`.

# Containers on storage backends

A [`TensorClass`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass) or a [`TypedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TypedTensorDict.html#tensordict.TypedTensorDict)
can wrap a tensordict on any storage backend without a copy. The backends are
an in-memory [`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict), an HDF5 or zarr file
([`PersistentTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.html#tensordict.PersistentTensorDict)), a Redis server
([`TensorDictStore`](reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore)), a lazy stack
([`LazyStackedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict.html#tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict)), or a memory-mapped
`TensorDict`. Code that uses the typed fields then reads and writes the file
or the server directly. A few operations behave differently on some backends:
see Operations on each backend.

`TypedTensorDict` is experimental: its API can change in a minor release
without a deprecation cycle (see [TypedTensorDict](typed_tensordict.html#typed-tensordict-guide)). To choose
between `TensorClass` and `TypedTensorDict`, see
[Which container should I use?](choosing_a_container.html#choosing-a-container). For the backends themselves, see [Large datasets and storage backends](storage.html#storage)
and [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving).

## How the classes relate

```
TensorDictBase
├── TensorDict (in memory)
├── TypedTensorDict (typed fields, wraps any TensorDictBase)
├── PersistentTensorDict (HDF5 or zarr file)
├── TensorDictStore (Redis, Dragonfly or KeyDB server)
└── LazyStackedTensorDict (lazy stack of tensordicts)

TensorClass (typed fields, has a TensorDictBase)
```

A `TypedTensorDict` is a [`TensorDictBase`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase). A
`TensorClass` is not: it keeps its fields in a tensordict that it holds.
Both have a `from_tensordict(td)` class method that wraps `td`. Reads and
writes through the wrapper go to the storage of `td`. If you call the
constructor instead, the storage is a new in-memory `TensorDict`.

## Operations on each backend

The following operations work on each backend, directly or through a
`TensorClass` or a `TypedTensorDict`, with the exceptions in the next
table:

- Build: `MyTC.from_tensordict(td)`.
- Read a field: `w.a`.
- Write a field: `w.a = value`.
- In-place write: `w.set_("a", value)` and `w.update(d, inplace=True)`.
- Update: `w.update(d)`.
- Index: `w[0]` returns the wrapper class, and `w[0] = other` writes
into the backend.
- Clone: `w.clone()`.
- Stack: `torch.stack([w, w])`.
- Iterate: `list(w)`.

| Backend | Operation | What happens, and what to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Memory-mapped `TensorDict` | Write a field, `update(d)` | `memmap_()` locks the tensordict, so these raise `RuntimeError: Cannot modify locked TensorDict`. Use `set_()`, `update_()`, or `update(d, inplace=True)`, which write into the existing files. |
| `PersistentTensorDict` | Write a field, `update(d)` | Each write replaces the dataset in the file and warns `UserWarning: Replacing an array with another one is inefficient`. To write into the existing dataset, use `set_()` or `update(d, inplace=True)`. |
| `PersistentTensorDict` | `clone()` | Without a destination, it warns `A destination should be provided when cloning a PersistentTensorDict`. An HDF5 clone goes to a temporary file that is not deleted. A zarr clone raises `FileExistsError`. Pass a destination: `w.clone(newfile=path)`. To copy the data into memory, use `to_tensordict()`. |
| `PersistentTensorDict` opened read-only (the default of `from_h5()` and `from_zarr()`) | In-place methods such as `add_()`, `update_(d)`, `copy_(d)` | Write nothing, and warn `FutureWarning: Calling add_() on a tensordict stored in a file opened read-only, which leaves the file unchanged, is deprecated and will be removed in TensorDict 0.17`. From 0.17 on, these calls raise, as `zero_()` and `set_()` already do. Open the file with `mode="r+"` to write, or call `to_tensordict()` to change a copy in memory. |
| `PersistentTensorDict`, `TensorDictStore`, `LazyStackedTensorDict` | In-place operation on a field, such as `w.a.add_(1)` | Reading an entry returns a new tensor with a copy of the data, so the operation does not change the storage. Write the result back with `w.a = ...`, `set_()`, or an indexed assignment. |

### Nested tensorclass fields

A field can have another tensorclass as its type (`a: Pose` or
`a: Pose | None`). If the input is a `TensorDict` and its entry for that
field is a tensordict, `from_tensordict` builds a `Pose` from that entry,
recursively. The `Pose` goes into a shallow copy of the input. The leaves
are shared, but the input keeps its tensordict entry, and it does not see the
entries set later on the tensorclass. An entry with keys that `Pose` does
not declare stays a tensordict. On the other backends, `from_tensordict`
wraps the input as it is, and the nested entry stays a tensordict, so that
the wrapper writes nothing to their storage.

## A TensorClass on each backend

The examples write their files to a temporary directory, and use this class:

```
>>> import tempfile
>>> tmpdir = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
>>> path = tmpdir.name
>>> import torch
>>> from torch import Tensor
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict, TensorClass
>>> class MyTC(TensorClass):
... a: Tensor
... b: Tensor
```

### In-memory `TensorDict`

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"a": torch.randn(4, 3), "b": torch.randn(4, 5)}, batch_size=[4])
>>> tc = MyTC.from_tensordict(td)
>>> tc.a.shape
torch.Size([4, 3])
```

### HDF5 (`PersistentTensorDict`)

```
>>> import os
>>> from tensordict import PersistentTensorDict
>>> h5 = PersistentTensorDict.from_dict(td, filename=os.path.join(path, "data.h5"))
>>> tc_h5 = MyTC.from_tensordict(h5)
>>> tc_h5.a.shape # reads from the HDF5 file
torch.Size([4, 3])
```

### Redis (`TensorDictStore`)

These examples need a Redis server on `localhost`, so the docs build does
not run them. To start a server for a test, run
`docker run --rm -d -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine`.

```
>>> from tensordict.store import TensorDictStore
>>> store = TensorDictStore.from_tensordict(td, host="localhost") 
>>> tc_redis = MyTC.from_tensordict(store) 
>>> tc_redis.a.shape # fetched from Redis 
torch.Size([4, 3])
```

The data stays on the server after the process ends. To delete it, call
`store.clear_redis()`. To close the connection, call `store.close()`:

```
>>> store.clear_redis() 
>>> store.close()
```

### Lazy stack

```
>>> from tensordict import lazy_stack
>>> tds = [TensorDict({"a": torch.randn(3), "b": torch.randn(5)}) for _ in range(4)]
>>> ls = lazy_stack(tds, dim=0)
>>> tc_lazy = MyTC.from_tensordict(ls)
>>> tc_lazy[0].a.shape
torch.Size([3])
```

### Memory-mapped `TensorDict`

`memmap_()` locks the tensordict, so write with `set_()`:

```
>>> td_mmap = td.clone().memmap_(os.path.join(path, "tc_memmap"))
>>> tc_mmap = MyTC.from_tensordict(td_mmap)
>>> tc_mmap.a.shape
torch.Size([4, 3])
>>> _ = tc_mmap.set_("a", torch.ones(4, 3))
>>> bool((td_mmap["a"] == 1).all())
True
```

### `TypedTensorDict`

A `TypedTensorDict` can be the backend of a `TensorClass`. Both declare
fields, and the two declarations do not conflict:

```
>>> from tensordict import TypedTensorDict
>>> class MyTTD(TypedTensorDict):
... a: Tensor
... b: Tensor
>>> ttd = MyTTD(a=torch.randn(4, 3), b=torch.randn(4, 5), batch_size=[4])
>>> tc_typed = MyTC.from_tensordict(ttd)
>>> tc_typed.a.shape
torch.Size([4, 3])
```

The other direction is not supported: `TypedTensorDict.from_tensordict`
accepts a tensorclass, but an attribute write through it raises
`ValueError`.

## A TypedTensorDict on each backend

The examples use this class:

```
>>> class State(TypedTensorDict):
... x: Tensor
... y: Tensor
```

### In-memory `TensorDict`

The constructor creates an in-memory `TensorDict`:

```
>>> state = State(x=torch.randn(4, 3), y=torch.randn(4, 5), batch_size=[4])
>>> state.x.shape
torch.Size([4, 3])
```

`from_tensordict` wraps an existing `TensorDict` without a copy:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"x": torch.randn(4, 3), "y": torch.randn(4, 5)}, batch_size=[4])
>>> state = State.from_tensordict(td)
>>> state.x.shape # reads from td
torch.Size([4, 3])
>>> state.x = torch.ones(4, 3) # writes to td
>>> (td["x"] == 1).all()
tensor(True)
```

### HDF5 (`PersistentTensorDict`)

```
>>> h5_state = PersistentTensorDict.from_dict(td, filename=os.path.join(path, "state.h5"))
>>> state = State.from_tensordict(h5_state)
>>> state.x.shape # reads from the HDF5 file
torch.Size([4, 3])
```

### Redis (`TensorDictStore`)

As above, these examples need a Redis server on `localhost`:

```
>>> store = TensorDictStore.from_tensordict(td, host="localhost") 
>>> state = State.from_tensordict(store) 
>>> state.x.shape # fetched from Redis 
torch.Size([4, 3])
>>> store.clear_redis() 
>>> store.close()
```

### Lazy stack

```
>>> tds = [TensorDict({"x": torch.randn(3), "y": torch.randn(5)}) for _ in range(4)]
>>> ls = lazy_stack(tds, dim=0)
>>> state = State.from_tensordict(ls)
>>> state[0].x.shape
torch.Size([3])
```

### Memory-mapped `TensorDict`

```
>>> td_mmap = td.clone().memmap_(os.path.join(path, "state_memmap"))
>>> state = State.from_tensordict(td_mmap)
>>> state.x.shape
torch.Size([4, 3])
>>> _ = state.set_("x", torch.zeros(4, 3))
>>> bool((td_mmap["x"] == 0).all())
True
```

### Stacking TypedTensorDicts

`torch.stack` returns an instance of the `TypedTensorDict` subclass:

```
>>> s1 = State(x=torch.randn(3), y=torch.randn(3), batch_size=[3])
>>> s2 = State(x=torch.randn(3), y=torch.randn(3), batch_size=[3])
>>> stacked = torch.stack([s1, s2], dim=0)
>>> type(stacked).__name__, stacked.batch_size
('State', torch.Size([2, 3]))
```

A lazy stack also works. An index of a `LazyStackedTensorDict` of
`TypedTensorDict` instances returns the subclass:

```
>>> from tensordict import LazyStackedTensorDict
>>> ls = LazyStackedTensorDict(s1, s2, stack_dim=0)
>>> isinstance(ls[0], State)
True
```

When you no longer need the files, close the HDF5 files and delete the
directory:

```
>>> h5.close()
>>> h5_state.close()
>>> tmpdir.cleanup()
```

To allocate storage on a Redis server first and fill it one sample at a time,
see [pre-allocating on Redis](storage.html#compat-redis-prealloc).

## See also

- [TensorClass](tensorclass.html#tensorclass-guide) and [TypedTensorDict](typed_tensordict.html#typed-tensordict-guide): the two typed

# torch.compile, torch.func, torch.export, and CUDA graphs

This page lists what works when tensordicts and tensorclasses go through
[`torch.compile()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.compile.html#torch.compile), [`torch.func`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/func.api.html#module-torch.func), [`torch.export.export()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/user_guide/torch_compiler/export/api_reference.html#torch.export.export), and CUDA
graphs, what makes a function recompile or fail, and how to work around each
limit.

## How tensordicts compile

[`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict), [`LazyStackedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict.html#tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict),
and tensorclasses are registered as pytree nodes, so [`torch.func`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/func.api.html#module-torch.func) and
[`torch.export.export()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/user_guide/torch_compiler/export/api_reference.html#torch.export.export) see their tensors as leaves. Inside
[`torch.compile()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.compile.html#torch.compile), Dynamo traces the Python code of tensordict like user
code: indexing, `apply`, arithmetic, reductions (see [Arithmetic, apply, reductions, and gradients](concepts/operations.html#operations)),
shape operations, stacking, and construction all end up in the graph. Most
operations compile with `fullgraph=True`. With that flag, a graph break
raises an error instead of splitting the function into several graphs.

```
>>> import torch
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict, tensorclass
>>> @tensorclass
... class Transition:
... obs: torch.Tensor
... reward: torch.Tensor
>>> @torch.compile(fullgraph=True)
... def scale(td):
... return td.apply(lambda x: x / x.abs().max()) * 2
>>> @torch.compile(fullgraph=True)
... def step(data):
... return Transition(data.obs + 1, data.reward * 0.5, batch_size=data.batch_size)
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "obs": torch.randn(8, 3),
... "next": TensorDict({"obs": torch.randn(8, 3)}, batch_size=[8]),
... },
... batch_size=[8],
... )
>>> scale(td).batch_size
torch.Size([8])
>>> step(Transition(torch.zeros(8, 3), torch.ones(8), batch_size=[8])).reward[0]
tensor(0.5000)
```

To find out why a function recompiles or breaks, run it with
`TORCH_LOGS="recompiles"` or `TORCH_LOGS="graph_breaks"` in the
environment, or call `torch._logging.set_logs(recompiles=True)` first.

## Recompiles

Dynamo specializes a compiled function on the structure of its inputs and
installs guards that check it on every call. A call that fails a guard
compiles the function again. By default, a function compiles at most 8 times
(`torch._dynamo.config.recompile_limit`). After that, it runs in eager mode,
or raises `FailOnRecompileLimitHit` with `fullgraph=True`. With
tensordicts, a function recompiles for the following reasons.

Another key set

An operation that goes over all the entries (arithmetic, `apply`,
`clone`, reductions) is compiled for the keys it saw. An input with another
key set compiles a new graph. Reading one entry (`td["obs"]`) does not
depend on the other keys.

Writing into an input tensordict

`td["y"] = ...`, `td.set`, `td.update`, and a
[`TensorDictModule`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule) (which writes its `out_keys` into
its input, see [Modules: TensorDictModule and tensordict.nn](modules.html#modules-guide)) recompile whenever the key set of the
input changes, even when the key written already exists. Dynamo guards on
all the keys of a dict that the function writes into
([#1606](https://github.com/pytorch/tensordict/issues/1606),
[pytorch/pytorch#175858](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/175858)).
A write into a nested tensordict only depends on the keys of that nested
tensordict. If the key sets vary, build a new tensordict in the compiled
function and write it into the input outside:

```
>>> @torch.compile(fullgraph=True)
... def policy(td):
... return TensorDict({"action": td["obs"].tanh()}, batch_size=td.batch_size)
>>> td = TensorDict({"obs": torch.randn(4, 3)}, batch_size=[4])
>>> td["action"] = policy(td)["action"]
```

Another batch size

The first call with a new batch size recompiles once with dynamic shapes
(automatic dynamic shapes), and later sizes reuse that graph.
`torch.compile(fn, dynamic=True)` avoids the second compilation.
`torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic` on an entry does not: the batch size holds
Python ints, and a function that builds a tensordict with
`batch_size=td.batch_size` then raises `ConstraintViolationError`.
`split`, `chunk`, `unbind`, and `tolist` recompile for each batch
size, also after that.

Lazy stacks of another length

A [`LazyStackedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict.html#tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict) is specialized on the number of
tensordicts it stacks, also with `dynamic=True`. A new stack of the same
length and structure reuses the graph.

Strings in the output

Each distinct `str` value of a tensorclass field or of a
[`NonTensorData`](reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData) entry (see [Non-tensor data and unbatched entries](concepts/non_tensor.html#non-tensor-data))
recompiles the function when the function returns it, for instance
through `apply`, `clone`, or the constructor of a tensorclass. Dynamo
specializes the graph on the value. Reading only the tensors does not
recompile. Return tensors from the
compiled function and rebuild the tensorclass outside, or keep the strings
out of the compiled function.

New tensorclasses and pytree flattening

A compiled function that flattens a tensordict as a pytree (a compiled
`torch.vmap`, `torch.utils._pytree.tree_map`) recompiles after a new
tensorclass or [`TypedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TypedTensorDict.html#tensordict.TypedTensorDict) subclass is defined,
because PyTorch guards on the size of its pytree registry. Define the
classes before the first call.

With `TORCH_LOGS="recompiles"`, the guard that failed names the cause. A
guard on `len(td._tensordict)` means that the key set of a tensordict that
the function writes into changed. A guard on `td._batch_size[0]` means a new
batch size.

## Known limits

The following patterns break the graph (an error with `fullgraph=True`).
The error messages in the table are those of PyTorch 2.13, 2.14, and the 2.16
nightly. Other versions can word them differently.

| Pattern | What happens | Workaround |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `td * t`, `t * td`, `td + t`, `td -= t` where `t` is a [`Tensor`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/tensors.html#torch.Tensor) (also with tensorclasses) | Dynamo turns the operator into a `Tensor` method and does not call `TensorDict.__mul__` ([pytorch/pytorch#200455](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/200455)): `Unsupported: All __torch_function__ overrides returned NotImplemented`. Operators with a Python number or another tensordict work. | Call the method: `td.mul(t)`, `td.add(t)`, `td.sub_(t)`. |
| `td.all()`, `td.any()` without `dim`, and `if (td == other).all():` | These return a Python `bool`, so the graph depends on tensor values: `Unsupported: Data-dependent branching`. | Reduce in the graph: `torch.stack([v.all() for v in td.values(include_nested=True, leaves_only=True)]).all()`, and select with [`torch.where()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.where.html#torch.where) instead of `if`. `td.all(dim=0)` returns a tensordict and compiles. |
| Boolean-mask indexing: `td[mask]`, `td[mask] = other[mask]` | The result has a data-dependent shape, also with `torch._dynamo.config.capture_dynamic_output_shape_ops = True`: `Could not guard on data-dependent expression`. | Keep the shapes fixed: `torch.where(mask, td, other)`, `td.where(mask, other)`, or `td.masked_fill(~mask, 0.0)`, or index outside the compiled function. |
| `memmap`, `memmap_like`, `share_memory_`, `to_namedtuple`, `data_ptr` | Eager-only operations (files, shared memory, Python classes built at run time). See [Devices, dtypes, and memory](concepts/devices.html#devices) and [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving). | Call them outside the compiled function. |
| `loss.backward()` or `torch.autograd.grad` inside the compiled function | Dynamo does not trace the backward pass: `Unsupported Tensor.backward() call`. | Return the loss and call `loss.backward()` outside. |
| Building a [`TensorDictSequential`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictSequential) inside the compiled function (`seq[:2](td)`, `seq.select_subsequence(...)`) | Dynamo cannot build the new module inside the graph: `Unexpected type in sourceless builder`. | Build the subsequence once, outside, and call it inside. |

PyTorch 2.11 and 2.12 also break the graph on `state_dict()`, as 2.14 does
([pytorch/pytorch#201124](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/201124)).
On PyTorch 2.12, building a frozen `tensor_only` tensorclass whose custom
`__init__` calls `object.__setattr__` raises `InternalTorchDynamoError`
inside a compiled function: build it outside.

## torch.func

[`torch.vmap()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.vmap.html#torch.vmap) maps over the batch dimensions of tensordicts and
tensorclasses: `in_dims` and `out_dims` refer to batch dimensions, and
tensordict methods, arithmetic included, work on the per-sample tensordict.
`torch.compile(torch.vmap(fn))` compiles the same code.

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"a": torch.randn(5, 3), "b": torch.randn(5, 3)}, batch_size=[5])
>>> torch.vmap(lambda t: (t * 2 + 1).exp())(td).batch_size
torch.Size([5])
>>> torch.vmap(lambda t, x: t["a"] @ x, (0, None))(td, torch.randn(3)).shape
torch.Size([5])
```

Under [`torch.func`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/func.api.html#module-torch.func) transforms, pointwise tensordict methods run one
operation per entry, so they are slower than in eager mode
([pytorch/pytorch#200456](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/200456)).

[`torch.func.grad()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.grad.html#torch.func.grad), [`grad_and_value()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.grad_and_value.html#torch.func.grad_and_value),
[`vjp()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.vjp.html#torch.func.vjp), and [`jacrev()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.jacrev.html#torch.func.jacrev) accept tensordict
inputs. The gradient is a tensordict with the structure of the input:

```
>>> grads = torch.func.grad(lambda t: (t["a"] ** 2).sum())(td)
>>> torch.testing.assert_close(grads["a"], 2 * td["a"])
```

For Jacobians and Hessians of functions that take and return tensordicts,
and for `torch.autograd.grad` and `backward` on tensordicts, see the
"Gradients" section of [Arithmetic, apply, reductions, and gradients](concepts/operations.html#operations).

To call a module with other parameters, extract them with
[`from_module()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict.from_module) and swap them in with
[`to_module()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_module.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_module). This works in eager mode, compiled,
and under [`torch.vmap()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.vmap.html#torch.vmap), which gives model ensembles and per-sample
gradients:

```
>>> from torch import nn
>>> module = nn.Linear(3, 1)
>>> def call(params, x):
... with params.to_module(module):
... return module(x)
>>> x = torch.randn(10, 3)
>>> ensemble = TensorDict.from_modules(*[nn.Linear(3, 1) for _ in range(4)])
>>> torch.vmap(call, (0, None))(ensemble, x).shape
torch.Size([4, 10, 1])
>>> def loss(params, x):
... return call(params, x).pow(2).sum()
>>> params = TensorDict.from_module(module).detach()
>>> per_sample = torch.vmap(torch.func.grad(loss), (None, 0))(params, x)
>>> per_sample["weight"].shape
torch.Size([10, 1, 3])
```

[`torch.func.functional_call()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.func.functional_call.html#torch.func.functional_call) only accepts a `dict`: pass
`params.flatten_keys(".").to_dict()` instead of the tensordict. See the
[Functional calls and ensembles with TensorDict](tutorials/functional.html) tutorial for more.

## torch.export

[`torch.export.export()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/user_guide/torch_compiler/export/api_reference.html#torch.export.export) accepts tensordict and tensorclass inputs and
outputs, in strict and non-strict mode (non-strict is the default). To keep
the batch dimension dynamic, give `dynamic_shapes` one entry per entry of
the tensordict, in the order of `td.keys()` (insertion order), with a nested
list for a nested tensordict:

```
>>> class Model(nn.Module):
... def forward(self, td):
... return TensorDict({"c": td["a"] * 2 + td["n", "b"]}, batch_size=td.batch_size)
>>> def make(batch):
... return TensorDict(
... {
... "a": torch.randn(batch, 3),
... "n": TensorDict({"b": torch.randn(batch, 3)}, batch_size=[batch]),
... },
... batch_size=[batch],
... )
>>> batch = torch.export.Dim("batch")
>>> program = torch.export.export(
... Model(), (make(4),), dynamic_shapes=([{0: batch}, [{0: batch}]],)
... )
>>> program.module()(make(6)).batch_size
torch.Size([6])
```

Without `dynamic_shapes`, a call with another batch size fails a guard of
the exported program (`AssertionError: Guard failed`). Both modes accept
tensordicts with dimension names or non-tensor entries.
To export a [`TensorDictModule`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule) so that it takes and
returns plain tensors, see the [Exporting tensordict modules](tutorials/export.html) tutorial.

## CUDA graphs

Two tools record CUDA graphs. [`CudaGraphModule`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.CudaGraphModule.html#tensordict.nn.CudaGraphModule) works
with or without [`torch.compile()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.compile.html#torch.compile), records one graph, and checks the
inputs of each call against it. `torch.compile(..., mode="reduce-overhead")`
needs compilation and manages its own graphs: it records a new graph for each
new batch size.

### CudaGraphModule

[`CudaGraphModule`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.CudaGraphModule.html#tensordict.nn.CudaGraphModule) captures a function, or a
[`TensorDictModule`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule), in a
[`torch.cuda.CUDAGraph`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.cuda.CUDAGraph.html#torch.cuda.CUDAGraph) and replays it. The function can be compiled.
Give it enough `warmup` calls to finish compiling, for instance
`CudaGraphModule(torch.compile(module), warmup=3)`. The first
`warmup - 1` calls (`warmup=2` by default) run the function on a side
stream. The next call runs it once more and captures the graph, and later
calls copy their inputs into the graph's buffers and replay it. See
[`CudaGraphModule`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.CudaGraphModule.html#tensordict.nn.CudaGraphModule) for the other requirements: no
data-dependent control flow, and inputs that do not require gradients.

```
>>> from tensordict.nn import CudaGraphModule, TensorDictModule
>>> module = TensorDictModule(lambda x: x + 1, in_keys=["x"], out_keys=["y"])
>>> graph_module = CudaGraphModule(module)
>>> results = [
... graph_module(TensorDict({"x": torch.full((3,), float(i), device="cuda")}, batch_size=[3]))
... for i in range(4)
... ]
>>> [result["y"][0].item() for result in results]
[1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]
```

The replay follows these rules:

- The inputs must keep the shapes and batch size of the capture. A
tensordict input without one of the `in_keys` raises a `KeyError`, and
a tensordict input with another batch size or entry shape raises a
`ValueError`, as a tensor input of another shape does. Extra keys are
ignored. After the capture, a CPU input is copied to the device.
- The outputs are new tensors: the values written into the input
tensordict, and the outputs of a function that returns a new tensordict or
tensors, are clones of the graph's buffers. A result kept from an earlier
call keeps its values.
- In-place writes to the inputs inside the function (`x.add_(1)`) do not
reach the caller's tensors after the capture: the graph writes its own
copies.
- The inputs are copied, and the graph replayed, on the current stream. If
the inputs are written on another stream, order that work before the call,
for instance with `torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(stream)`.
Issue consecutive calls from one stream, or order them in the same way.
- Arguments that are not tensors (a `float`, a `str`) must not change
after the capture. If the function takes a tensordict, the replay uses the
captured values, ignores the new ones and emits a `FutureWarning`.
Starting with TensorDict 0.17, the default will change to raising a
`ValueError` (pytorch/tensordict#2075). Every tensor must be an entry of
the tensordict, not a separate argument. If the function takes tensors, a
changed value raises a `ValueError`.

### `mode="reduce-overhead"`

`torch.compile(module, mode="reduce-overhead")` records CUDA graphs with
the cudagraph trees of Inductor. It works with tensordict inputs and outputs,
and the PyTorch rules apply:

- The output tensors of a call are overwritten by the next call. Reading them
afterwards raises `RuntimeError: Error: accessing tensor output of
CUDAGraphs that has been overwritten by a subsequent run`. Clone the
outputs that you keep (`out = compiled(td).clone()`).
- A function that writes in place into an input tensor (`td["x"].add_(1)`)
runs without CUDA graphs (`skipping cudagraphs due to mutated inputs` with
`TORCH_LOGS="cudagraphs"`).
- For inference, call the function under [`torch.no_grad`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.no_grad.html#torch.no_grad). With
gradients enabled and no backward pass, the calls run without recording a
CUDA graph (`Running eager function` with `TORCH_LOGS="cudagraphs"`).

For example:

```
>>> policy = torch.compile(
... TensorDictModule(nn.Linear(3, 4).cuda(), in_keys=["obs"], out_keys=["action"]),
... mode="reduce-overhead",
... )
>>> with torch.no_grad():
... outputs = [
... policy(TensorDict({"obs": torch.randn(8, 3, device="cuda")}, batch_size=[8])).clone()
... for _ in range(4)
... ]
>>> outputs[0]["action"].shape
torch.Size([8, 4])
```

- [Arithmetic, apply, reductions, and gradients](concepts/operations.html#operations): arithmetic, `apply`, reductions, and gradients with
tensordicts.
- [Modules: TensorDictModule and tensordict.nn](modules.html#modules-guide): [`TensorDictModule`](reference/generated/tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule.html#tensordict.nn.TensorDictModule) and the
other modules of `tensordict.nn`.
- [Devices, dtypes, and memory](concepts/devices.html#devices): `to()`, pinned memory, and shared memory.
- [FX tracing (prototype)](fx.html#fx): FX tracing of tensordict modules, a prototype.

# Batch size, shapes, and indexing

The batch size is the shape that all the entries of a
[`TensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict) share at the front. With it, one index, one
`reshape`, or one `unbind` applies to every tensor of the group. A tensor
of the wrong shape raises an error when you add it.

## Batch size and batch dimensions

The leading dimensions that all the entries share are the batch dimensions.
`batch_dims` is their number. The dimensions that come after them are the
feature dimensions of each entry, and they can differ from entry to entry.

In this example, a tensordict holds 3 time steps of 2 robots. Each robot has
4 joint angles and one battery level:

```
>>> import torch
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "joints": torch.zeros(2, 3, 4),
... "battery": torch.zeros(2, 3),
... },
... batch_size=[2, 3],
... )
>>> td.batch_size
torch.Size([2, 3])
>>> td.batch_dims
2
>>> td["joints"].shape[td.batch_dims:] # the feature dimensions of "joints"
torch.Size([4])
>>> td["battery"].shape[td.batch_dims:]
torch.Size([])
```

`td.shape` and `td.size()` return the batch size. `td.ndim` and
`td.dim()` return `batch_dims`. `td.numel()` is the number of elements
in the batch (here 6), not the number of values in the tensors.

A [`TensorClass`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass) has a batch size too, with the same rules
for its typed fields (see [TensorClass](../tensorclass.html#tensorclass-guide)).

The leading dimensions of each entry must be equal to the batch size. If they
are not, the constructor and each write raise a `RuntimeError` that names the
key:

```
>>> td["contact"] = torch.zeros(3)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: batch dimension mismatch, got self.batch_size=torch.Size([2, 3]) and value.shape=torch.Size([3]) for key 'contact'. The leading dimensions of a value must match the batch size.
```

TensorDict stores a Python number as a 0-dim tensor. If the batch size is not
empty, a number therefore gives the same error. To store one number for each
element, expand it to the batch size. To store one number for the whole batch,
see [Non-tensor data and unbatched entries](non_tensor.html#non-tensor-data).

```
>>> td["contact"] = torch.tensor(False).expand(td.batch_size)
>>> td["contact"].shape
torch.Size([2, 3])
```

A nested tensordict is an entry too. Its batch size must start with the batch
size of its parent, and it can have more batch dimensions. When you give a
dictionary as a value, the nested tensordict gets the batch size of the parent:

```
>>> td["target"] = {"joints": torch.zeros(2, 3, 4)}
>>> td["target"].batch_size
torch.Size([2, 3])
```

To store a tensor that does not have the batch dimensions, wrap it in an
[`UnbatchedTensor`](../reference/generated/tensordict.UnbatchedTensor.html#tensordict.UnbatchedTensor) (see [UnbatchedTensor](non_tensor.html#unbatched-tensor)).

## Empty batch size

If you do not give a batch size, it is `torch.Size([])`: no batch
dimensions. TensorDict does not infer it from the entries. With an empty batch
size, the entries can have any shape, but you cannot index the tensordict or
iterate over it:

```
>>> data = TensorDict({"images": torch.zeros(3, 4), "labels": torch.zeros(3)})
>>> data.batch_size
torch.Size([])
>>> data[0]
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: indexing a tensordict with td.batch_dims==0 is not permitted. Got index 0.
```

`TensorDict()` creates a tensordict with no entries and an empty batch size.

## Infer the batch size

To infer the batch size from the entries, do one of these:

- Pass `auto_batch_size=True` to [`from_dict()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_dict.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_dict).
- Call [`auto_batch_size_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.auto_batch_size_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.auto_batch_size_) on an existing
tensordict. It changes the tensordict and returns it.

Both set the batch size to the longest list of leading dimensions that all the
entries share. Use `batch_dims` to set a maximum number of batch dimensions:

```
>>> TensorDict.from_dict(
... {"images": torch.zeros(3, 4), "labels": torch.zeros(3)}, auto_batch_size=True
... ).batch_size
torch.Size([3])
>>> data = TensorDict({"images": torch.zeros(3, 4, 5), "masks": torch.zeros(3, 4)})
>>> data.auto_batch_size_().batch_size
torch.Size([3, 4])
>>> data.auto_batch_size_(batch_dims=1).batch_size
torch.Size([3])
```

`auto_batch_size_` also gives each nested tensordict the longest batch size
of its own entries.

## Change the batch size

You can assign a new batch size if all the entries are compatible with it. An
empty batch size is always compatible:

```
>>> data = TensorDict({"images": torch.zeros(3, 4)}, batch_size=[3])
>>> data.batch_size = [3, 4]
>>> data.batch_size = [4]
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: the Tensor images has shape torch.Size([3, 4]) which is incompatible with the batch-size torch.Size([4]).
```

A [`LazyStackedTensorDict`](../reference/generated/tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict.html#tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict) (see [Stacking and variable-size data](stacking.html#stacking)) does not
accept a new batch size, not even an empty one. Call
[`to_tensordict()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_tensordict.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_tensordict) first.

## Indexing

An index on a TensorDict follows one rule:

- A string, or a tuple of strings, reads one entry (see [Keys, nested keys, and locking](keys.html#keys)).
- Any other index applies to the batch dimensions of all the entries at once:
an integer, a slice, `...`, `None`, a list or tensor of integers, or a
boolean mask.

The result of a batch index is a TensorDict. Because the index applies to the
batch dimensions, `td[..., :2]["joints"]` and `td["joints"][..., :2]` are
different:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"joints": torch.zeros(2, 3, 4), "battery": torch.zeros(2, 3)}, batch_size=[2, 3])
>>> td[0].batch_size # robot 0, all time steps
torch.Size([3])
>>> td[..., :2]["joints"].shape # the first 2 time steps
torch.Size([2, 2, 4])
>>> td["joints"][..., :2].shape # the first 2 joints
torch.Size([2, 3, 2])
>>> td[:, None].batch_size
torch.Size([2, 1, 3])
```

A boolean mask selects elements of the leading batch dimensions, as for a
tensor. Its shape must match those dimensions:

```
>>> mask = torch.tensor([[True, False, True], [False, False, True]])
>>> td[mask].batch_size
torch.Size([3])
>>> td[mask]["joints"].shape
torch.Size([3, 4])
>>> td[torch.tensor([True, False])].batch_size
torch.Size([1, 3])
```

A list of strings is not a key selection. To keep some keys, use
[`select()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.select.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.select) (see [Keys, nested keys, and locking](keys.html#keys)).

Indexing follows the rules of [`torch`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/torch.html#module-torch) for storage. An integer or a slice
gives views, so an in-place change of an entry of the result changes the
original. A mask or a tensor of indices gives copies. A new key that you write
into the result does not appear in the original:

```
>>> sub = td[0]
>>> sub["battery"] += 1
>>> td["battery"]
tensor([[1., 1., 1.],
 [0., 0., 0.]])
>>> sub["new"] = torch.zeros(3)
>>> "new" in td
False
```

To write into the batch elements of the original, assign to an index. The
value can be a TensorDict with the batch size of the indexed result, or a
number or tensor that broadcasts to each entry:

```
>>> td[1] = TensorDict({"joints": torch.ones(3, 4), "battery": torch.ones(3)}, batch_size=[3])
>>> td[:, 0] = 0
>>> td["battery"]
tensor([[0., 1., 1.],
 [0., 1., 1.]])
```

If you write a TensorDict into an index of an empty tensordict, the first write
creates the entries. See [Lazy pre-allocation](stacking.html#stacking-preallocation).

## Shape operations

The shape operations of a TensorDict apply the same operation to the batch
dimensions of each entry. They do not change the feature dimensions, and their
dimension arguments count batch dimensions only:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"joints": torch.zeros(2, 3, 4), "battery": torch.zeros(2, 3)}, batch_size=[2, 3])
>>> td.reshape(6)["joints"].shape
torch.Size([6, 4])
>>> td.permute(1, 0)["joints"].shape
torch.Size([3, 2, 4])
>>> td.unsqueeze(-1)["joints"].shape # a new last batch dimension, before the 4 joints
torch.Size([2, 3, 1, 4])
>>> td.flatten(0, 1).unflatten(0, (2, 3)).batch_size
torch.Size([2, 3])
>>> [t.batch_size for t in td.unbind(1)]
[torch.Size([2]), torch.Size([2]), torch.Size([2])]
>>> [t.batch_size for t in td.split([2, 1], dim=1)]
[torch.Size([2, 2]), torch.Size([2, 1])]
```

The other shape operations are [`view()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.view.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.view),
[`transpose()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.transpose.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.transpose),
[`squeeze()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.squeeze.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.squeeze),
[`expand()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.expand.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.expand),
[`chunk()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.chunk.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.chunk), [`repeat()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.repeat.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.repeat),
and [`repeat_interleave()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.repeat_interleave.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.repeat_interleave). As for tensors,
`view`, `permute`, `unbind`, and `expand` return views of the same
storage. `expand` repeats the same memory, so an in-place write into an
expanded entry raises a `RuntimeError`. Call `clone()` first to get
separate copies.

To join tensordicts with [`torch.stack()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.stack.html#torch.stack) and [`torch.cat()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.cat.html#torch.cat), see
[Stacking and variable-size data](stacking.html#stacking).

## Dimension names

You can give a name to each batch dimension, as with the named tensors of
PyTorch. `names` has one entry for each batch dimension, and `None` means
that the dimension has no name. Give the names at construction, or set them
later:

```
>>> td = TensorDict(batch_size=[3, 4], names=["robot", None])
>>> td.names
['robot', None]
>>> td = td.refine_names(..., "time")
>>> td.names
['robot', 'time']
>>> td.names = ["env", "step"]
>>> td = td.rename("agent", "t")
>>> td.names
['agent', 't']
>>> td = td.rename(agent="robot")
>>> td.names
['robot', 't']
```

The names follow the shape operations:

```
>>> td[0].names # indexing removes the name of the indexed dimension
['t']
>>> td.permute(1, 0).names
['t', 'robot']
>>> td.unsqueeze(0).names # a new dimension has no name
[None, 'robot', 't']
>>> td.reshape(12).names
[None]
```

If the number of names is not `batch_dims`, TensorDict raises a `ValueError`.
A nested tensordict has the names of its parent for the shared batch
dimensions. The shape operations take dimension numbers, not names.

## A TensorDict is not *exactly* a dict

A [`dict`](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict) is a good model of a TensorDict. A TensorDict has the
mapping methods of a dict: `keys()`, `values()`, `items()`, `get()`,
`pop()`, `update()`, and `setdefault()`, and it unpacks with `**td`.
The operations below are the exceptions. Most of them follow the rules of a
tensor:

Iteration

`for x in td` iterates over the first batch dimension, like a tensor. Each
`x` is a TensorDict. A tensordict with no batch dimensions raises a
`TypeError`. To iterate over the entries, use `keys()`, `values()`, or
`items()`.

`len`

`len(td)` is the size of the first batch dimension, or 0 if the batch size
is empty. `len(td.keys())` is the number of keys.

`bool`

`bool(td)`, `if td:`, and `while td:` raise a `RuntimeError`, so
that `assert td1 == td2` cannot pass by accident. To test for keys, use
`len(td.keys())`. [`is_empty()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.is_empty.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.is_empty) tests for
leaves: a tensordict that holds only empty sub-tensordicts is empty. To
reduce a comparison, use `(td1 == td2).all()` or `.any()`.

`in`

`key in td` tests the keys, as for a dict. A tuple of strings tests a
nested key.

`==`

`td == other` compares each entry and returns a TensorDict of booleans,
like a tensor. If the two tensordicts do not have the same keys, it raises a
`KeyError`. Call `.all()` on the result to get a Python `bool`.
`td in some_list` uses `==`, so it raises unless `td` itself is in the
list. A TensorDict is not hashable.

For example:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"a": torch.arange(3), "nested": {"b": torch.zeros(3, 2)}}, batch_size=[3])
>>> [x.batch_size for x in td]
[torch.Size([]), torch.Size([]), torch.Size([])]
>>> len(td), len(td.keys())
(3, 2)
>>> bool(td)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: Converting a tensordict to boolean value is not permitted
>>> td.is_empty()
False
>>> "a" in td, ("nested", "b") in td, "b" in td
(True, True, False)
>>> (td == td.clone()).all()
True
```

If a dataset returns tensordicts with no batch dimensions, the default collate
function of [`torch.utils.data.DataLoader`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/data.html#torch.utils.data.DataLoader) iterates over them and raises
the same `TypeError`. [Load data and share it between processes](../data_loading.html#data-loading) gives the `collate_fn` to use.

## See also

- [`batch_size`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.batch_size.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.batch_size),
[`auto_batch_size_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.auto_batch_size_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.auto_batch_size_),
[`from_dict()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_dict.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_dict), and
[`names`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.names.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.names) in the [API reference](../reference/index.html#api-reference).
- [Indexing, masking, and splitting](../reference/td.html#api-methods-indexing) and [Shape, batch dimensions, and stacking](../reference/td.html#api-methods-shape): the indexing and
shape methods.
- The tutorials [Slicing, indexing, and masking](../tutorials/tensordict_slicing.html) and
[Changing the shape of a TensorDict](../tutorials/tensordict_shapes.html).

# Devices, dtypes, and memory

One call moves or casts every tensor of a tensordict, nested ones too:
`td.to("cuda")`, `td.to(torch.float16)`, or a device and a dtype for each
tensor, copied from another tensordict. The `device` attribute of the
tensordict also decides where new entries go.

Most examples use the `meta` device in place of a GPU. Every PyTorch build
has it: a tensor on the `meta` device has a shape and a dtype, but no data.
The examples that need a CUDA device are marked `+SKIP`.

## Move and cast with `to()`

[`to()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.to.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.to) takes the same arguments as
[`torch.Tensor.to()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.Tensor.to.html#torch.Tensor.to), and applies them to each leaf (each tensor at the end
of a key path). It returns a new tensordict, and sets its `device` attribute
(see The device of a tensordict) when you give a device:

```
>>> import torch
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict
>>> batch = TensorDict({"images": torch.zeros(4, 3, 8, 8), "labels": torch.arange(4)}, batch_size=[4])
>>> batch.to("meta").device
device(type='meta')
>>> batch64 = batch.to(torch.float64)
>>> batch64["images"].dtype, batch64["labels"].dtype
(torch.float64, torch.float64)
>>> both = batch.to("meta", torch.float16)
>>> both["images"].device, both["images"].dtype
(device(type='meta'), torch.float16)
```

A dtype casts every leaf, also the integer and boolean leaves, such as
`labels` here. To cast only some of them, see Per-leaf device and dtype
casting. These forms also work:

- `td.to(tensor)` uses the device and the dtype of `tensor`.
- `td.to(other=other_td)` uses the device of `other_td`, and its dtype if
all its leaves have one dtype.
- [`float()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.float.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.float), [`double()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.double.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.double),
[`half()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.half.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.half), [`int()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.int.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.int),
[`bool()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.bool.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.bool), and the other dtype methods of
[`torch.Tensor`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/tensors.html#torch.Tensor) cast every leaf.
- [`cpu()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.cpu.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.cpu) and [`cuda()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.cuda.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.cuda)
are the same as `to("cpu")` and `to("cuda")`.

If the tensordict already has the target device and you give no dtype,
`to()` returns the same tensordict. With `inplace=True`, `to()` writes
the cast leaves into the same tensordict and returns it.

The `non_blocking` argument controls how the leaves are copied:

- `None` (the default): the leaves are copied with `non_blocking=True`.
If the target device is not a CUDA device (for example, the CPU), `to()`
then synchronizes once, after all the copies. If the target is the CPU,
`to()` synchronizes only if a leaf comes from another device.
Under [`torch.compile()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.compile.html#torch.compile), these copies are blocking.
- `True`: the copies are non-blocking and `to()` does not synchronize.
You must synchronize before you read the data.
- `False`: the copies are blocking.

With `non_blocking_pin=True`, `to()` pins each leaf (see Pinned
memory) before the copy, in `num_threads` threads. This needs an
accelerator.

### Temporary moves

`to()` also works as a context manager. In the `with` block, you work on
the moved or cast tensordict. At the end of the block, the values go back
into the entries of the original tensordict, which keep their original device
and dtype. The entries that the block adds are added to
the original tensordict too. They keep the dtype that they have in the block.
If the original tensordict has a device, they go to that device:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"x": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3], device="cpu")
>>> with td.to(torch.float64) as td64:
... td64["x"] += 1
... td64["y"] = td64["x"] * 2
>>> td["x"]
tensor([1., 1., 1.])
>>> td["y"].dtype
torch.float64
```

With a GPU, the same pattern runs one step on the GPU and keeps the results
on the CPU. This example needs a CUDA device:

```
>>> def op(td):
... return td + 1
>>> td_cpu = TensorDict({"x": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3], device="cpu")
>>> with td_cpu.to("cuda:0") as td_gpu: 
... td_gpu.update(op(td_gpu))
>>> td_cpu.device 
device(type='cpu')
>>> bool((td_cpu == 1).all()) 
True
```

## The device of a tensordict

A tensordict has a [`device`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.device.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.device) attribute. By
default, it is `None`, also if all the leaves are on the same device:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3])
>>> print(td.device)
None
```

The value changes what happens to the entries that you add:

- If `device` is a device, each entry that you add, at construction or
later, is moved to that device. Nested tensordicts get the same device.
- If `device` is `None`, each entry keeps its device. The leaves can be
on different devices.

In this example, `td` has the `meta` device, and `mixed` has no device:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3], device="meta")
>>> td["b"] = torch.ones(3) # a CPU tensor
>>> td["b"].device
device(type='meta')
>>> td["n"] = {"c": torch.ones(3)}
>>> td["n"].device, td["n", "c"].device
(device(type='meta'), device(type='meta'))
>>> mixed = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(3), "b": torch.zeros(3, device="meta")}, batch_size=[3])
>>> print(mixed.device)
None
```

Two methods change the attribute and do not move any leaf:

- [`auto_device_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.auto_device_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.auto_device_) sets `device` to the device
of the leaves if they are all on one device, and to `None` otherwise.
- [`clear_device_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.clear_device_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.clear_device_) sets `device` to `None`.

Here, all the leaves are on the CPU:

```
>>> TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3]).auto_device_().device
device(type='cpu')
```

## Per-leaf device and dtype casting

If a tensordict has `device=None`, its leaves can be on different devices
and have different dtypes. `td.to(device)` moves all the leaves to one
device. To give each leaf the device and the dtype of the matching leaf in
another tensordict, pass the result of
[`attrs()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.attrs.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.attrs) to `to()`. Use this, for example, to
match FSDP or tensor-parallel shards, data from other ranks, or a
mixed-precision state dict.

[`attrs()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.attrs.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.attrs) returns a tensordict whose leaves are
[`TensorAttrs`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorAttrs.html#tensordict.TensorAttrs) objects, one for each leaf. Each one records
the device, the dtype, and the shape of its leaf. `to()` casts each leaf of
the tensordict to the device and the dtype of the leaf with the same key in
this spec:

```
>>> source = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(3), "b": torch.zeros(3, dtype=torch.float64)}, batch_size=[3])
>>> layout = TensorDict(
... {
... "a": torch.zeros(3, dtype=torch.float16, device="meta"),
... "b": torch.zeros(3, dtype=torch.float32),
... },
... batch_size=[3],
... )
>>> out = source.to(layout.attrs())
>>> out["a"].device, out["a"].dtype
(device(type='meta'), torch.float16)
>>> out["b"].device, out["b"].dtype
(device(type='cpu'), torch.float32)
```

On a machine with two GPUs, the same call moves each leaf to its own GPU or
to the CPU:

```
>>> td0 = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(3, device="cuda:0"), 
... "b": torch.zeros(3, device="cpu")}, batch_size=[3])
>>> td2 = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(3, device="cpu"), 
... "b": torch.zeros(3, device="cuda:1")}, batch_size=[3])
>>> td3 = td0.to(td2.attrs()) 
>>> td3["a"].device, td3["b"].device 
(device(type='cpu'), device(type='cuda', index=1))
```

These rules apply:

- By default, the copies are asynchronous. If at least one leaf moves from an
accelerator to the CPU (D2H, device to host), `to()` synchronizes once at
the end. Copies to an accelerator (H2D) or between accelerators (D2D) do not
need it, because later kernels on the destination device wait for the copy.
- With `non_blocking=True`, `to()` does not synchronize. You must
synchronize before you read the data on the host.
- With `non_blocking=False`, the copies are blocking.
- A spec that changes only dtypes never synchronizes.
- Leaves that are not in the spec do not change. A partial spec changes only
some leaves.
- `attrs(fields=...)` selects the attributes that each
[`TensorAttrs`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorAttrs.html#tensordict.TensorAttrs) records. The default is
`("device", "dtype", "shape")`. `to()` uses only the device and the
dtype. With `fields=("dtype",)`, the spec changes only the dtypes.
- `non_blocking_pin=True` is not supported with a spec. It raises
`NotImplementedError`.

In this example, the spec has only the key `"a"`, so `"b"` keeps its dtype:

```
>>> partial = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(3, dtype=torch.float16)}, batch_size=[3]).attrs()
>>> out = source.to(partial)
>>> out["a"].dtype, out["b"].dtype
(torch.float16, torch.float64)
```

For the rules of non-blocking copies and pinned memory in PyTorch, see the
PyTorch tutorial
[A Guide on Good Usage of non_blocking and pin_memory()](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/intermediate/pinmem_nonblock.html).

## Pinned memory

Pinned (page-locked) CPU memory makes copies from the CPU to a GPU faster,
and lets them run asynchronously. [`pin_memory()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.pin_memory.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.pin_memory)
returns a tensordict whose leaves are in pinned memory. With
`inplace=True`, it replaces the leaves of the same tensordict.
`num_threads` sets the number of threads that pin the leaves. The default
(`None`) uses many threads, and `num_threads=0` pins on the main thread.
Pinning needs an accelerator, so this example does not run on a CPU-only
machine:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"pos": torch.zeros(64, 3)}, batch_size=[64])
>>> pinned = td.pin_memory() 
>>> td_gpu = pinned.to("cuda", non_blocking=True)
```

`td.to("cuda", non_blocking_pin=True)` pins and copies in one call. In this
form, the pinning is asynchronous: threads pin the leaves while the copies
run. With `td.pin_memory().to("cuda")`, all the leaves are pinned before
the first copy starts. Starting the threads has a fixed cost on every call,
so the one-call form pays off only for large tensordicts, with leaves of a
MiB or more and tens of MiB in total. For smaller ones, a plain
`td.to("cuda")` is usually faster than either form.
[`pin_memory_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.pin_memory_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.pin_memory_) is deprecated, and will be removed
in version 0.17. Use `pin_memory(inplace=True)`.

## Shared memory

[`share_memory_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.share_memory_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.share_memory_) moves each CPU leaf to shared
memory. Other processes on the same machine can then read and write the
leaves without a copy, for example the workers of
[`torch.multiprocessing`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/multiprocessing.html#module-torch.multiprocessing). After this call, the tensordict is locked (see
[Locking and temporary changes](keys.html#keys-locking)). You can write into the existing leaves, but you cannot
add, remove, or replace an entry:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3]).share_memory_()
>>> td.is_shared(), td.is_locked
(True, True)
>>> td["b"] = torch.zeros(3)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: Cannot modify locked TensorDict. ...
>>> _ = td.set_("a", torch.ones(3))
>>> td["a"][0] = 5.0
>>> td["a"]
tensor([5., 1., 1.])
```

`share_memory_()` keeps non-tensor values of built-in types, such as ints,
floats, bools, strings, bytes, lists and dicts. Two cases lose data and warn.
A shared string has a fixed size, the size of its first value and at least
100 bytes: `update_` with a longer string stores only its first bytes. A
shared integer holds the signed 64-bit range, and an integer outside it
wraps: `2**63` reads back as `-2**63`.
[Load data and share it between processes](../data_loading.html#data-loading) shows how to share tensordicts between processes.

## Consolidation

[`consolidate()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate) copies all the leaves into one
contiguous storage, and makes each leaf a view of it. `to(device)` on a
consolidated tensordict then copies one buffer instead of one tensor for
each leaf, and the result is consolidated too. For the same reason, a
consolidated tensordict is faster to send to another process. The result of
`consolidate()` is locked. If you call
[`unlock_()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.unlock_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.unlock_) on it, it is no longer consolidated:

```
>>> c = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(3), "b": torch.ones(3, 2)}, batch_size=[3]).consolidate()
>>> c.is_consolidated(), c.is_locked
(True, True)
>>> c.to("meta").is_consolidated()
True
```

[Save and load tensordicts](../saving.html#saving) describes consolidation for serialization.

[`pin_memory()`](../reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.pin_memory.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.pin_memory), and the other methods on this
page.

`share_memory_()` and `memmap_()` do not follow.
