### Keys, values, and entries

Read, write, select, and rename the entries of a tensordict. A key is a
string, or a tuple of strings that points to an entry of a nested
tensordict. [`NestedKey`](generated/tensordict.NestedKey.html#tensordict.NestedKey) is the type of these keys. For the rules,
see [Keys, nested keys, and locking](../concepts/keys.html#keys). For values that are not tensors, see
[Non-tensor data and unbatched entries](../concepts/non_tensor.html#non-tensor-data).

### Indexing, masking, and splitting

Index every entry along the batch dimensions at once, and split a
tensordict into several tensordicts. `td[0]` and `td[mask]` index the
batch dimensions. `td["key"]` returns an entry: see
Keys, values, and entries. For the rules, see [Batch size, shapes, and indexing](../concepts/batch_size.html#batch-size).

| [`TensorDictBase.__getitem__`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.__getitem__.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.__getitem__)() | Indexes all tensors according to the provided index. |

### Shape, batch dimensions, and stacking

Read and change the batch size and the dimension names, reshape and expand
a tensordict, and stack or concatenate several tensordicts. These methods
change the batch dimensions. The dimensions of each entry after the batch
dimensions do not change. See [Batch size, shapes, and indexing](../concepts/batch_size.html#batch-size) and [Stacking and variable-size data](../concepts/stacking.html#stacking).

`to` and the dtype shorthands take a `cast_filter` predicate
`fn(key, value) -> bool` that selects the leaves to cast. The predicates
below test the dtype of their last argument, so they serve as a
`cast_filter` and as a test in [`apply()`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply).

### Pointwise math

Apply arithmetic and elementwise functions to every entry. The Python
operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `**`, `==`, `&`, ...) call
these methods. A method whose name ends with an underscore, such as
`add_`, writes into the existing tensors: see
[In-place operations](../concepts/operations.html#inplace-conventions). For broadcasting and for tensordicts with
different keys, see [Arithmetic, apply, reductions, and gradients](../concepts/operations.html#operations).

Arithmetic

| [`TensorDictBase.add`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.add.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.add)(other, *[, alpha, default]) | Adds `other`, scaled by `alpha`, to `self`. |
| --- | --- |
| [`TensorDictBase.add_`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.add_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.add_)(other, *[, alpha]) | In-place version of [`add()`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.add.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.add). |
| [`TensorDictBase.sub`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.sub.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.sub)(other, *[, alpha, default]) | Subtracts `other`, scaled by `alpha`, from `self`. |
| [`TensorDictBase.sub_`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.sub_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.sub_)(other[, alpha]) | In-place version of [`sub()`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.sub.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.sub). |
| [`TensorDictBase.rsub`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.rsub.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.rsub)(other, *[, alpha, default]) | Subtracts `self`, scaled by `alpha`, from `other`, leaf by leaf. |
| [`TensorDictBase.mul`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.mul.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.mul)(other, *[, default]) | Multiplies `other` to `self`. |
| [`TensorDictBase.mul_`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.mul_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.mul_)(other) | In-place version of [`mul()`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.mul.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.mul). |
| [`TensorDictBase.div`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.div.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.div)(other, *[, default]) | Divides each element of the input `self` by the corresponding element of `other`. |
| [`TensorDictBase.div_`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.div_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.div_)(other) | In-place version of [`div()`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.div.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.div). |

### Reductions

Reduce each entry over all its elements, or along batch dimensions with
`dim`. With `reduce=True`, most reductions return one tensor for the
whole tensordict. See [Arithmetic, apply, reductions, and gradients](../concepts/operations.html#operations).

| [`TensorDictBase.all`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.all.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.all)([dim]) | Checks if all values are True/non-null in the tensordict. |
| --- | --- |
| [`TensorDictBase.any`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.any.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.any)([dim]) | Checks if any value is True/non-null in the tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.amax`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.amax.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.amax)([dim, keepdim, reduce]) | Returns the maximum values of all elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.amin`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.amin.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.amin)([dim, keepdim, reduce]) | Returns the minimum values of all elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.max`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.max.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.max)([dim, keepdim, reduce, ...]) | Returns the maximum values of all elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.min`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.min.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.min)([dim, keepdim, reduce, ...]) | Returns the minimum values of all elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.cummax`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.cummax.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.cummax)(dim, *[, reduce, ...]) | Returns the cumulative maximum values of all elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.cummin`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.cummin.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.cummin)(dim, *[, reduce, ...]) | Returns the cumulative minimum values of all elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.mean`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.mean.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.mean)([dim, keepdim, dtype, ...]) | Returns the mean value of all elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.nanmean`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.nanmean.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.nanmean)([dim, keepdim, ...]) | Returns the mean of all non-NaN elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.sum`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.sum.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.sum)([dim, keepdim, dtype, ...]) | Returns the sum value of all elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.nansum`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.nansum.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.nansum)([dim, keepdim, dtype, ...]) | Returns the sum of all non-NaN elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.prod`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.prod.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.prod)([dim, keepdim, dtype, ...]) | Returns the produce of values of all elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.std`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.std.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.std)([dim, keepdim, ...]) | Returns the standard deviation value of all elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.var`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.var.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.var)([dim, keepdim, ...]) | Returns the variance value of all elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.quantile`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.quantile.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.quantile)(q[, dim, keepdim, ...]) | Returns the q-th quantile of all elements in the input tensordict. |
| [`TensorDictBase.logsumexp`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.logsumexp.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.logsumexp)([dim, keepdim, out]) | Returns the log of summed exponentials of each row of the input tensordict in the given dimension `dim`. |
| [`TensorDictBase.norm`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.norm.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.norm)(*[, out, dtype, ...]) | Computes the norm of each tensor in the tensordict. |

### Apply, modules, and gradients

Apply a function to every entry, and map a function over the batch. Put
the parameters of a module in a tensordict and back, and compute
gradients.
See [Arithmetic, apply, reductions, and gradients](../concepts/operations.html#operations), [Modules: TensorDictModule and tensordict.nn](../modules.html#modules-guide), and [torch.compile, torch.func, torch.export, and CUDA graphs](../compile.html#compile).

Methods

| [`TensorDictBase.apply`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.apply)(fn, *others[, ...]) | Applies a callable to all values stored in the tensordict and sets them in a new tensordict. |

### Saving, loading, and file formats

Save a tensordict to disk and load it again, and write its entries to
memory-mapped files. Other methods read and write key-value stores, and HDF5,
zarr, CSV, JSON, Parquet, and MDS files.
`memmap(return_early=True)` returns a
[`TensorDictFuture`](generated/tensordict.utils.TensorDictFuture.html#tensordict.utils.TensorDictFuture). See [Save and load tensordicts](../saving.html#saving) and
[Large datasets and storage backends](../storage.html#storage).

### Locking

A locked tensordict raises an error if you add, replace, rename, or delete
an entry. In-place writes with `set_` and `update_` still work, also for
non-tensor entries. `unlock_` also works in a `with` block: the
tensordict is locked again at the end of the block. See [Keys, nested keys, and locking](../concepts/keys.html#keys).

| [`TensorDictBase.lock_`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.lock_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.lock_)() | Locks the tensordict and its sub-tensordicts, and returns it. |
| --- | --- |
| [`TensorDictBase.unlock_`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.unlock_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.unlock_)() | Unlocks the tensordict and its sub-tensordicts, and returns it. |
| [`TensorDictBase.is_locked`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.is_locked.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.is_locked) | `True` if the tensordict is locked. |

## Package constants

tensordict.KEY_SEPARATOR

`"."`, the default `separator` of
[`flatten_keys()`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.flatten_keys.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.flatten_keys) and
[`unflatten_keys()`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.unflatten_keys.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.unflatten_keys), for code that joins or
splits nested keys the same way, such as
`tuple(name.split(KEY_SEPARATOR))`. The names of
[`state_dict()`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.state_dict.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.state_dict) also use `"."`, the
`torch.nn.Module` convention, independently of this constant.
Reassigning it has no effect: the defaults are bound when the methods are
defined. It can also be imported from `tensordict.utils`.

tensordict.base.NO_DEFAULT

The sentinel that marks an argument as not given where `None` is a valid
value, such as `default` in [`get_non_tensor()`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.get_non_tensor.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.get_non_tensor)
or `device` in [`new_zeros()`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.new_zeros.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.new_zeros). It can also
be imported from `tensordict.tensordict`.

tensordict.__version__

The version string of the installed tensordict package, or `None` if it
cannot be determined, for example when tensordict is imported from a source
tree that is not installed.

# TypedTensorDict

Warning

`TypedTensorDict` is experimental: its API can change in a minor release
without a deprecation cycle.

This page lists [`TypedTensorDict`](generated/tensordict.TypedTensorDict.html#tensordict.TypedTensorDict), a
[`TensorDictBase`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase) subclass whose fields you declare as
class annotations, as in a `TypedDict`. A subclass adds fields to the
fields of its parent, and [`from_tensordict()`](generated/tensordict.TypedTensorDict.html#tensordict.TypedTensorDict.from_tensordict)
wraps any tensordict (H5, Redis, lazy stacks) without a copy. For a guide
with examples, see [TypedTensorDict](../typed_tensordict.html#typed-tensordict-guide).

`TypedTensorDict` has the methods of [`TensorDictBase`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase),
listed by task in [Methods by task](td.html#api-tensordict-methods).

| [`TypedTensorDict`](generated/tensordict.TypedTensorDict.html#tensordict.TypedTensorDict)(*args, **kwargs) | A TensorDictBase subclass with typed field declarations and backend composition. |
| --- | --- |

## See also

- [TypedTensorDict](../typed_tensordict.html#typed-tensordict-guide): declare and use a `TypedTensorDict`.
- [Which container should I use?](../choosing_a_container.html#choosing-a-container): tensorclass, `TypedTensorDict`, or
`TensorDict`.
- [Containers on storage backends](../compatibility.html#compatibility): which containers work on which storage backends.

# Utilities

This page lists the names of `tensordict.utils` that the `tensordict`
module does not export: helpers for tensors and tensordicts, the types
that some methods return, and type aliases. Import them from
`tensordict.utils`. The names that `tensordict` also exports, such as
[`unravel_key()`](generated/tensordict.unravel_key.html#tensordict.unravel_key) or [`assert_close()`](generated/tensordict.assert_close.html#tensordict.assert_close), are
on [tensordict: containers and functions](td.html#api-tensordict).

## Tensor and tensordict helpers

`expand_right` and `expand_as_right` add dimensions on the right of a
tensor, where broadcasting adds them on the left. `isin` and
`remove_duplicates` compare the values of one entry along a batch
dimension.

| [`expand_right`](generated/tensordict.utils.expand_right.html#tensordict.utils.expand_right)(tensor, shape) | Expand a tensor on the right to match a desired shape. |
| --- | --- |
| [`expand_as_right`](generated/tensordict.utils.expand_as_right.html#tensordict.utils.expand_as_right)(tensor, dest) | Expand a tensor on the right to match another tensor shape. |
| [`isin`](generated/tensordict.utils.isin.html#tensordict.utils.isin)(input, reference, key[, dim]) | Tests if each element of `key` in input `dim` is also present in the reference. |
| [`remove_duplicates`](generated/tensordict.utils.remove_duplicates.html#tensordict.utils.remove_duplicates)(input, key[, dim, ...]) | Removes indices duplicated in key along the specified dimension. |

## Returned types

The methods that have a `return_early` argument, such as
[`memmap()`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap), return a
[`TensorDictFuture`](generated/tensordict.utils.TensorDictFuture.html#tensordict.utils.TensorDictFuture) if you pass `return_early=True`.
[`tolist()`](generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.tolist.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.tolist) returns
a [`LinkedList`](generated/tensordict.utils.LinkedList.html#tensordict.utils.LinkedList) if you pass `as_linked_list=True`.

| [`TensorDictFuture`](generated/tensordict.utils.TensorDictFuture.html#tensordict.utils.TensorDictFuture)(futures, resulting_td) | A custom future class for TensorDict multithreaded operations. |
| --- | --- |
| [`LinkedList`](generated/tensordict.utils.LinkedList.html#tensordict.utils.LinkedList)(*args, td, **kwargs) | A list of the values of a non-tensor entry that writes item assignments back to the tensordict. |

| --- | --- |

## Debugging and profiling

`print_directory_tree` prints the files of a directory, for example
the directory of a saved tensordict. `timeit` and `logger` are the
timer and the logger that tensordict uses in its own code. `Buffer` is
[`torch.nn.Buffer`](generated/tensordict.utils.Buffer.html#tensordict.utils.Buffer), kept here so that old
imports of `tensordict.utils.Buffer` still work.

| [`print_directory_tree`](generated/tensordict.utils.print_directory_tree.html#tensordict.utils.print_directory_tree)(path[, indent, ...]) | Prints the directory tree starting from the specified path. |
| --- | --- |
| [`timeit`](generated/tensordict.utils.timeit.html#tensordict.utils.timeit)(name) | Measures the time spent in a function or a block of code, by name. |
| [`Buffer`](generated/tensordict.utils.Buffer.html#tensordict.utils.Buffer)([data, persistent]) | A kind of Tensor that should not be considered a model parameter. |

tensordict.utils.logger

The [`logging.Logger`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html#logging.Logger) named `"tensordict"`. To show fewer
messages from tensordict, raise the level of this logger, for example
`logging.getLogger("tensordict").setLevel(logging.WARNING)`.

# Save and load tensordicts

[`save()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.save.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.save) writes each tensor of a tensordict
(each *leaf*) to its own file, in a directory tree that follows the keys.
[`load_memmap()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap) maps the files back into
memory, and reads a leaf from disk only when you use it. Here, one call saves
the state of 100 particles:

```
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> import torch
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict
>>> tmp = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
>>> root = Path(tmp.name)
>>> particles = TensorDict(
... {"pos": torch.zeros(100, 3), "vel": torch.ones(100, 3)}, batch_size=[100]
... )
>>> _ = particles.save(root / "particles")
>>> loaded = TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "particles")
>>> loaded[0]["vel"]
MemoryMappedTensor([1., 1., 1.])
```

The examples on this page run in order, and share the temporary directory
`root`.

## Choose a format

| To do this | Use | Section |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Save a model checkpoint, then load all of it or one sub-module | [`save()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.save.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.save), [`load_memmap()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap) | Save a checkpoint |
| Give the data to someone as one file that loads lazily | `td.save("data.tdz")` | Single-file archives |
| Open or pickle the data in the shortest time | [`consolidate()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate), [`from_consolidated()`](reference/generated/tensordict.from_consolidated.html#tensordict.from_consolidated) | Consolidated files |
| Give the file to code that calls [`torch.load()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.load.html#torch.load) | [`torch.save()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.save.html#torch.save) | torch.save and torch.load |
| Give the tensors to code that expects a flat state dict | [`state_dict()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.state_dict.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.state_dict) | state_dict and load_state_dict |
| Load a file that you did not write | `allow_pickle`, `weights_only` | Load data that you did not write |
| Preallocate a dataset on disk and fill it one sample at a time | [`memmap_like()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap_like.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap_like), [`from_schema()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_schema.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_schema) | [Large datasets and storage backends](storage.html#storage) |
| Store chunked, compressed, or remote data (HDF5, zarr, Redis) | [`PersistentTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.html#tensordict.PersistentTensorDict), [`TensorDictStore`](reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore) | [Large datasets and storage backends](storage.html#storage) |

## Save a checkpoint

To save a model, collect its parameters and buffers with
[`from_module()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_module.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_module). The result has one nested
tensordict for each sub-module:

```
>>> from torch import nn
>>> _ = torch.manual_seed(0)
>>> model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 4), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(4, 2))
>>> params = TensorDict.from_module(model)
>>> _ = params.save(root / "checkpoint")
>>> sorted(p.name for p in (root / "checkpoint").iterdir())
['0', '2', 'meta.json']
```

To load the checkpoint into a model, read it with `load_memmap`, and call
[`to_module()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_module.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_module) with `inplace=True`. It copies
each value into the existing parameter of the model, so the parameters stay
[`Parameter`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.parameter.Parameter.html#torch.nn.parameter.Parameter) instances in memory:

```
>>> new_model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 4), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(4, 2))
>>> loaded = TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "checkpoint")
>>> _ = loaded.to_module(new_model, inplace=True)
>>> torch.equal(new_model[0].weight, model[0].weight)
True
```

The loaded leaves are [`MemoryMappedTensor`](reference/generated/tensordict.MemoryMappedTensor.html#tensordict.MemoryMappedTensor) instances.
Without `inplace=True`, `to_module` makes a new parameter from each of
them, and the new parameter uses the file as its storage. If the files are
mapped as shared (`mode="r+"`, the default for a directory that you can
write), a change to the parameter, for example an optimizer step, changes
the checkpoint on disk.

To load one sub-module, pass its key as `subpath`. tensordict then reads
only that part of the tree. `subpath` takes a nested key, such as
`("encoder", "0")`, or a path, such as `"encoder/0"`:

```
>>> last_layer = TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "checkpoint", subpath="2")
>>> _ = last_layer.to_module(new_model[2], inplace=True)
>>> last_layer["weight"].shape
torch.Size([2, 4])
```

To read the keys, shapes, and dtypes of a checkpoint without its data, load
it on the `"meta"` device:

```
>>> TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "checkpoint", device="meta")["0", "weight"]
tensor(..., device='meta', size=(4, 3))
```

## Options of save and load_memmap

The methods have several names:

- [`save()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.save.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.save),
[`dumps()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.dumps.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.dumps), and
[`memmap()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap) are one method. They return a
new tensordict with memory-mapped leaves.
- [`memmap_()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap_) writes the same files, and
replaces the leaves of the tensordict itself.
- [`load()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.load.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.load) and
[`load_memmap()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap) are one method.

`memmap`, `memmap_`, and `save` lock the tensordict that they return.
You can write into its tensors in place, but you cannot add, remove, or
replace an entry (see [Locking and temporary changes](concepts/keys.html#keys-locking)).

To write several files at the same time, pass `num_threads`. Threads make
the save faster when the tensordict has a few large leaves, and slower when
it has many small ones. In one measurement, `num_threads=4` saved the
weights of [`torch.nn.Transformer`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Transformer.html#torch.nn.Transformer) (184 leaves, 168 MiB) 1.6 times as
fast as one thread, and saved 2000 small leaves 3 times as slowly. Measure
both on your data.

If you do not give a path, `memmap` and `memmap_` put each tensor in an
anonymous temporary file. On Linux, the file is in shared memory
(`/dev/shm`) if it has room. The file has no name, so `load_memmap`
cannot read it, and the data disappears when the process ends. Use this to
share data between processes (see [Load data and share it between processes](data_loading.html#data-loading)).

### Tensors that already have a file

If a leaf is already a memory-mapped tensor, `memmap` without a path keeps
the same tensor:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"a": 1}, [])
>>> td0 = td.memmap()
>>> td1 = td0.memmap()
>>> td0["a"] is td1["a"]
True
```

If you give another path, `memmap` raises an error, so that you do not copy
a large file by accident. To copy the file, pass `copy_existing=True`:

```
>>> td0 = td.memmap(root / "first")
>>> td1 = td0.memmap(root / "second")
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: A filename was provided but the tensor already has a file associated (...). To copy the tensor onto the new location, pass copy_existing=True.
>>> td1 = td0.memmap(root / "second", copy_existing=True)
>>> TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "second")["a"]
MemoryMappedTensor(1)
```

### Write to the files after you load them

The `mode` argument of `load_memmap` sets where an in-place change to a
loaded tensor goes:

- Default (`mode=None`): if the process can write the file, in-place
writes go to the file. If it cannot, the file loads as with `"r"`.
- `mode="r"`: the files are mapped copy-on-write. In-place writes stay in
memory, and the files do not change.
- `mode="r+"`: in-place writes go to the files. If a file is not writable,
`load_memmap` raises a `PermissionError`.

Here, the reader with `mode="r"` changes memory only, and the writer with
the default mode changes the file:

```
>>> _ = TensorDict({"a": torch.zeros(3)}, batch_size=[3]).save(root / "data")
>>> reader = TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "data", mode="r")
>>> _ = reader["a"].add_(1)
>>> TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "data")["a"]
MemoryMappedTensor([0., 0., 0.])
>>> writer = TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "data")
>>> _ = writer["a"].add_(1)
>>> TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "data")["a"]
MemoryMappedTensor([1., 1., 1.])
```

If many nodes read the same files on a network file system, load with
`mode="r"`. On some of these file systems (for example Lustre), a page
fault on a shared writable mapping takes a write lock. Readers on
different nodes then block each other. On Linux, a copy-on-write mapping
counts against the memory commit limit. If a file is larger than RAM plus
swap, `mode="r"` can fail to map it. In that case, use the default mode.

## Save to one file

A directory has one file for each leaf. To write one file instead, use an
archive, a consolidated file, or [`torch.save()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.save.html#torch.save):

| Format | Write, then read | Lazy load | Load one sub-tree | Use it to |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Archive (`.tdz`) | `td.save("x.tdz")`, `TensorDict.load_memmap("x.tdz")` | Yes | Yes (`subpath`) | Give a checkpoint or a dataset to other people, or copy it to a network file system |
| Consolidated file | `td.consolidate("x.bin")`, `from_consolidated("x.bin")` | Yes | No | Open the data in the shortest time |
| `torch.save` | `torch.save(td, "x.pt")`, `torch.load("x.pt")` | With `torch.load(..., mmap=True)` | No | Give the data to code that calls `torch.load` |

### Single-file archives

If the path ends with `".tdz"`, or if you pass `archive=True`,
[`save()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.save.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.save) (and `memmap` and `dumps`) writes
one file instead of a directory. This example saves a triangle mesh with a
temperature field on its vertices:

```
>>> mesh = TensorDict(
... {
... "vertices": torch.rand(10, 3),
... "faces": torch.randint(10, (16, 3)),
... "fields": {"temperature": torch.rand(10)},
... },
... )
>>> _ = mesh.save(root / "mesh.tdz")
>>> loaded = TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "mesh.tdz")
>>> (loaded == mesh).all()
True
```

The archive is a standard zip file. Its entries are the files of the
directory tree (the `meta.json` files and the `*.memmap` tensor files).
The tensor payloads are aligned and not compressed, so `load_memmap` maps
the archive once and makes each leaf a view into the mapping. Apart from
the metadata, tensordict reads a tensor from disk only when you use it.

Because the entries are the directory tree, you can convert an archive to a
directory and back, with [`pack_memmap()`](reference/generated/tensordict.pack_memmap.html#tensordict.pack_memmap) and
[`unpack_memmap()`](reference/generated/tensordict.unpack_memmap.html#tensordict.unpack_memmap) or with any zip tool:

```
unzip data.tdz -d data_dir # gives a directory that load_memmap reads
(cd data_dir && zip -0 -r ../data.zip .) # gives an archive that load_memmap reads
```

`subpath` works as with a directory. tensordict then reads only that part
of the archive:

```
>>> TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "mesh.tdz", subpath="fields")["temperature"].shape
torch.Size([10])
```

An archive loads differently from a directory in two ways:

- By default, the leaves are views into one storage, as with
[`from_consolidated()`](reference/generated/tensordict.from_consolidated.html#tensordict.from_consolidated). In-place writes change memory only,
not the file. To write to the file, load with `mode="r+"`.
- An archive made by another zip tool loads correctly. If a payload is not
aligned, tensordict copies that leaf into memory instead of making a view.

This example writes zeros to the archive through `mode="r+"`:

```
>>> mesh_rw = TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "mesh.tdz", mode="r+")
>>> _ = mesh_rw["vertices"].zero_()
>>> TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "mesh.tdz")["vertices"].sum()
tensor(0.)
```

An in-place write does not update the CRC-32 checksum that the zip format
stores for each entry. `load_memmap` does not read the checksums. Before
you give a changed archive to a tool that reads them, such as `unzip` or
[`unpack_memmap()`](reference/generated/tensordict.unpack_memmap.html#tensordict.unpack_memmap), call
[`refresh_archive_checksums()`](reference/generated/tensordict.refresh_archive_checksums.html#tensordict.refresh_archive_checksums):

```
>>> from tensordict import refresh_archive_checksums
>>> _ = refresh_archive_checksums(root / "mesh.tdz")
```

To compress an archive, pass `compression="deflate"`, `"bzip2"`, or
`"lzma"`. tensordict cannot memory-map a compressed leaf. It decompresses
the leaf into memory the first time you use it, and `mode="r+"` raises an
error. Use compression for archival storage. `uint8` images and boolean
masks compress well, and float weights do not.

### Consolidated files

[`consolidate()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate) copies all the leaves into one
contiguous storage, and makes each leaf a view into it. With a file name, the
storage is a memory-mapped file. [`from_consolidated()`](reference/generated/tensordict.from_consolidated.html#tensordict.from_consolidated) opens
the file again. This example saves a graph with four nodes and three edges:

```
>>> from tensordict import from_consolidated
>>> graph = TensorDict(
... {
... "nodes": torch.zeros(4, 8),
... "edges": {"index": torch.tensor([[0, 1, 2], [1, 2, 3]]), "weight": torch.ones(3)},
... },
... )
>>> graph_c = graph.consolidate(root / "graph.bin")
>>> from_consolidated(root / "graph.bin")["edges", "index"]
tensor([[0, 1, 2],
 [1, 2, 3]])
```

The file keeps the batch sizes and names that the tensordict had when
`consolidate` wrote it. If you change them on `graph_c` later, call
`graph_c.consolidate(root / "graph.bin")` again to write them into the file.

`consolidate` returns a locked tensordict. If you unlock it with
[`unlock_()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.unlock_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.unlock_), it is no longer consolidated:

```
>>> graph_c.is_locked, graph_c.is_consolidated()
(True, True)
>>> graph_c.unlock_().is_consolidated()
False
```

A consolidated tensordict also pickles faster, because pickle gets one
storage instead of one tensor for each leaf. In one measurement, pickling a
tensordict with 1000 small leaves took 34 ms, and 0.3 ms once consolidated
(`consolidate()` itself took 9 ms). [Distributed tensordicts](distributed.html#distributed) uses the same
layout to send a tensordict as one message. See
[`consolidate()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.consolidate) for its other options
(`num_threads`, `device`, `pin_memory`, `share_memory`).

## torch.save and torch.load

[`torch.load()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.load.html#torch.load) reads a tensordict that [`torch.save()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.save.html#torch.save) wrote, with
`weights_only=True` (the default since PyTorch 2.6). When you import
tensordict, it allowlists the classes and functions that these files
reference, with [`torch.serialization.add_safe_globals()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/serialization.html#torch.serialization.add_safe_globals). The list covers
[`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict), [`LazyStackedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict.html#tensordict.LazyStackedTensorDict),
consolidated tensordicts, non-tensor values made of Python builtins, such
as strings, numbers, lists, and dicts, and the `torch.return_types` that
`max(dim=...)`, `min(dim=...)`, `cummax` and `cummin` return:

```
>>> batch = TensorDict({"loss": torch.zeros(3), "meta": {"split": "train"}}, batch_size=[3])
>>> torch.save(batch, root / "batch.pt")
>>> torch.load(root / "batch.pt", weights_only=True)["meta", "split"]
'train'
```

The list does not include tensorclasses, or the types of other non-tensor
values, such as NumPy arrays or dates. For these, loading stops with an
`Unsupported global` error that names the missing class or function:

```
>>> import datetime
>>> from tensordict import NonTensorData
>>> td = TensorDict({"date": NonTensorData(datetime.date(2024, 1, 1))})
>>> torch.save(td, root / "date.pt")
>>> torch.load(root / "date.pt", weights_only=True)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
_pickle.UnpicklingError: Weights only load failed...Unsupported global: GLOBAL datetime.date was not an allowed global by default...
```

If the file comes from a source that you trust, allowlist the class. For a
tensorclass, allowlist the tensorclass:

```
>>> with torch.serialization.safe_globals([datetime.date]):
... td = torch.load(root / "date.pt", weights_only=True)
>>> td["date"]
datetime.date(2024, 1, 1)
```

`weights_only=True` cannot load a tensordict with
[`MemoryMappedTensor`](reference/generated/tensordict.MemoryMappedTensor.html#tensordict.MemoryMappedTensor) leaves. Save it with
[`save()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.save.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.save) and load it with
[`load_memmap()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_memmap) instead.

## state_dict and load_state_dict

[`state_dict()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.state_dict.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.state_dict) and
[`load_state_dict()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_state_dict.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.load_state_dict) follow the conventions of
[`torch.nn.Module.state_dict()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.Module.html#torch.nn.Module.state_dict). By default, `state_dict()` returns a
flat [`OrderedDict`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html#collections.OrderedDict) with dot-separated keys, as
`nn.Module` does:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"a": 1, "b": {"c": 2}}, [])
>>> sd = td.state_dict()
>>> dict(sd)
{'a': tensor(1), 'b.c': tensor(2)}
```

The metadata (`batch_size`, `device`) is in the `_metadata` attribute of
the returned `OrderedDict`, as in `nn.Module`. It has one entry for each
dot-separated prefix: `""` for the root, and `"b"` for the nested
tensordict at key `"b"`. It replaces the old `__batch_size` and
`__device` keys.

To get a nested state dict, pass `flatten=False`:

```
>>> sd_nested = td.state_dict(flatten=False)
>>> {key: dict(value) if isinstance(value, dict) else value for key, value in sd_nested.items()}
{'a': tensor(1), 'b': {'c': tensor(2)}}
```

`load_state_dict` reads each of the three formats: flat (with
`_metadata` and dot-separated keys), nested (with `_metadata` at each
level), and the old format (with `__batch_size` and `__device` keys):

```
>>> td_zero = td.clone().zero_()
>>> _ = td_zero.load_state_dict(sd)
>>> (td_zero == td).all()
True
>>> _ = td_zero.zero_().load_state_dict(sd_nested)
>>> (td_zero == td).all()
True
```

For a tensorclass, the keys of `state_dict()` are the names of the tensor
fields. The non-tensor fields are in `_metadata`:

```
>>> from tensordict import tensorclass
>>> @tensorclass
... class Labeled:
... x: torch.Tensor
... label: str
>>> sd = Labeled(x=torch.randn(3), label="hello", batch_size=[]).state_dict()
>>> list(sd.keys())
['x']
>>> sd._metadata[""]["_non_tensor"]
{'label': 'hello'}
```

## Load data that you did not write

Pickle can run any code when it loads a file. tensordict uses pickle in two
places on disk: the `other.pickle` files of a saved directory or archive,
and [`torch.save()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.save.html#torch.save) files.

Non-tensor values, such as strings, are in
[`NonTensorData`](reference/generated/tensordict.NonTensorData.html#tensordict.NonTensorData) entries or in tensorclass fields (see
[Non-tensor data and unbatched entries](concepts/non_tensor.html#non-tensor-data)). When you save them, tensordict writes the values that
JSON can represent to `meta.json`, and the other values to an
`other.pickle` file next to it:

```
>>> run = TensorDict(
... {
... "x": torch.zeros(3),
... "config": NonTensorData({"lr": 0.1}),
... "date": NonTensorData(datetime.date(2024, 1, 1)),
... },
... batch_size=[3],
... )
>>> _ = run.save(root / "run")
>>> sorted(p.name for p in (root / "run" / "config").iterdir())
['meta.json']
>>> sorted(p.name for p in (root / "run" / "date").iterdir())
['meta.json', 'other.pickle']
```

The `allow_pickle` argument of `load_memmap` sets whether tensordict loads
the `other.pickle` files:

- `allow_pickle=False`: if the data has a pickle file, `load_memmap`
raises a `RuntimeError`. Use this for data from a source that you do not
trust.
- `allow_pickle=True`: `load_memmap` loads the pickle files. Use this only
for data from a source that you trust.
- No value: tensordict 0.14 and 0.15 load the pickle files and emit a
`FutureWarning`. The default changes to `False` in tensordict 0.16.

The `date` value of the example above is in a pickle file:

```
>>> TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "run", allow_pickle=False)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: Refusing to load pickled non-tensor data from a memory-mapped TensorDict. ...
>>> TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "run", allow_pickle=True)["date"]
datetime.date(2024, 1, 1)
```

Data without a pickle file loads with `allow_pickle=False`. So does the
output of [`from_pytree()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_pytree.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_pytree), such as a module
`state_dict()`, when its containers are only `dict`,
`collections.OrderedDict`, `list` and `tuple`: tensordict pickles these
classes for older versions, and also saves their names in a
`json_types.json` file, which `load_memmap` reads instead of the pickle
file. Other classes, such as namedtuples, and the stacked results of
`from_pytree` (for example after [`torch.stack()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.stack.html#torch.stack)) load only from the
pickle file. `load_memmap_` and `memmap_refresh_` take the same
argument. For [`torch.load()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.load.html#torch.load), keep `weights_only=True` and allowlist
only the classes that you trust (see torch.save and torch.load).

A module `state_dict()` round-trips this way:

```
>>> model = torch.nn.Linear(2, 2)
>>> _ = TensorDict.from_pytree(model.state_dict()).memmap(root / "model")
>>> sd = TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "model", allow_pickle=False).to_pytree()
>>> all(torch.equal(sd[k], v) for k, v in model.state_dict().items())
True
```

The state dicts of an optimizer and of a learning-rate scheduler hold
`None`, `str` values and Python numbers, which `from_pytree` rejects
(`None` and `str` leaves) or returns as tensors (numbers). Save them with
[`torch.save()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.save.html#torch.save) and load them with `torch.load(path, weights_only=True)`,
which round-trips them exactly without unpickling arbitrary objects:

```
>>> optim = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
>>> model(torch.randn(3, 2)).sum().backward()
>>> optim.step()
>>> torch.save(optim.state_dict(), root / "optim.pt")
>>> optim_sd = torch.load(root / "optim.pt", weights_only=True)
>>> optim_sd["param_groups"] == optim.state_dict()["param_groups"]
True
>>> optim_sd["param_groups"][0]["foreach"] is None
True
>>> torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters()).load_state_dict(optim_sd)
```

The zarr backend has a separate, additive `allow_pickle` read policy on
`from_zarr` and `PersistentTensorDict`. `False` rejects pickle before
decoding; `True` permits it for trusted data; the current default,
`None`, reads it with a `FutureWarning` only when a pickled field is
accessed. Starting with TensorDict 0.17, the default will change to
`allow_pickle=False` for zarr. This does not change the memory-mapped
loader's 0.16 schedule. Tensor and JSON zarr entries need no opt-in.
See [zarr](storage.html#storage-zarr) for the policy of newly written stores.

tensordict also protects the paths that it writes:

- If the path of a new leaf file is a symbolic link, tensordict raises an
error. It cannot stop another process that renames files in the parent
directory at the same time. Keep the save directory, or the parent
directory of an archive, writable only by users that you trust. Use
[`tempfile.TemporaryDirectory`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/tempfile.html#tempfile.TemporaryDirectory) or another private directory, not a
fixed name in a shared `/tmp`.
- tensordict encodes the keys so that every file stays inside the save
directory, also for keys that contain `/` or `..`. `robust_key=False`
turns this off for old layouts. Do not use it with keys or metadata that
you do not trust.
- A save overwrites a leaf file that exists. To get an error instead, pass
`existsok=False`. `save` still rewrites the metadata files of a
directory that it reuses.

Two other features unpickle what they receive: the Redis backend of
[`TensorDictStore`](reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore) (see [Share data between nodes with Redis](storage.html#storage-redis)) and the
metadata of the `torch.distributed` methods (see
[Collectives](distributed.html#distributed-collectives)).

## The directory layout

The directory tree follows the keys: each leaf is a `*.memmap` file, and
each nested tensordict is a sub-directory. The `meta.json` file of each
directory holds what `load_memmap` needs to rebuild that level: the batch
size, the device, the shape and dtype of each leaf, the class of the
tensordict, and the non-tensor values that JSON can represent:

```
>>> td = TensorDict({"a": torch.rand(10), "b": {"c": torch.rand(10)}}, [10])
>>> _ = td.memmap_(root / "tree")
>>> sorted(str(p.relative_to(root / "tree")) for p in (root / "tree").rglob("*"))
['a.memmap', 'b', 'b/c.memmap', 'b/meta.json', 'meta.json']
```

Because `meta.json` stores the class of each level, `load_memmap` rebuilds
nested structures whose levels have different types, such as a tensorclass
inside a [`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict) or a stack of tensordicts:

```
>>> td_list = [TensorDict({"item": i}, batch_size=[]) for i in range(4)]
>>> @tensorclass
... class Record:
... data: torch.Tensor
... metadata: str
>>> data = TensorDict(
... {
... "td_list": torch.stack(td_list),
... "record": Record(torch.randn(3), metadata="some text", batch_size=[]),
... },
... )
>>> _ = data.memmap_(root / "mixed")
>>> loaded = TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "mixed")
>>> type(loaded["record"]) is Record
True
>>> loaded["record"].metadata
'some text'
```

[`print_directory_tree()`](reference/generated/tensordict.utils.print_directory_tree.html#tensordict.utils.print_directory_tree) logs the tree and its size
through the `tensordict` logger, and returns it as a string.

JSON cannot represent a `set`, so `save` writes a `set` value to an
`other.pickle` file. To load it, pass `allow_pickle=True` (see
Load data that you did not write). To keep the value in `meta.json`,
convert it to a list first.

## Memory-mapped tensors

A [`MemoryMappedTensor`](reference/generated/tensordict.MemoryMappedTensor.html#tensordict.MemoryMappedTensor) is a tensor whose data is in a file
on disk. It has constructors like those of torch, such as `empty`,
`zeros`, and `from_tensor`, and tensordict manages the file. Use it:

- To work with contiguous data that is larger than the memory.
- To send data to other processes. If all the processes can read the same
file, a memory-mapped tensor is sent as a file name and the metadata to
rebuild it. An indexed memory-mapped tensor is sent the same way if its
storage is still that of the original tensor.
- To read a few items. Indexing reads only those items, which is faster
than opening many separate files.

Apart from its file, you create and index a memory-mapped tensor like a
regular tensor:

```
>>> from tensordict import MemoryMappedTensor
>>> images = MemoryMappedTensor.empty(
... (100, 3, 64, 64), dtype=torch.uint8, filename=root / "images.memmap"
... )
>>> mini_batch = images[:10] # a view on the first 10 images
>>> # open the file again, here or in another process
>>> images = MemoryMappedTensor.from_filename(
... root / "images.memmap", dtype=torch.uint8, shape=(100, 3, 64, 64)
... )
>>> images.shape
torch.Size([100, 3, 64, 64])
```

## Speed

All the formats that this page describes, and safetensors, load lazily
through `mmap`. Reading all the data takes about the same time with each
of them. The differences come from a cost for each leaf, so they grow with
the number of leaves. In one run of
`benchmarks/scripts/serialization_formats_bench.py` with 100 MB of data:

- Open: a single file parses one metadata block, and a directory opens one
file for each leaf. With 2000 leaves, opening took 122 ms for a directory,
50 ms for an archive, and 13 ms for a consolidated file.
- Save: a directory save is the fastest. With 8 leaves, an archive took 25
times as long as a directory (845 ms and 34 ms). With 2000 leaves, it took
3.4 times as long.
- Copy: a directory has a cost for each file, and on a network file system
this cost grows with the round-trip time. With 2000 leaves, copying a
directory took 112 ms, and copying a single file took 34 to 51 ms.
- zarr ([`to_zarr()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_zarr.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_zarr)) does not memory-map,
and costs one round trip to the store for each leaf. [zarr](storage.html#storage-zarr)
gives its numbers.

The benchmark measures `torch.save` and safetensors on their fastest path:
a flat dict of tensors, loaded with
`torch.load(mmap=True, weights_only=True)` and with the memory-mapped
loader of safetensors. Neither format stores the tensordict structure: the
benchmark flattens the keys before the save, and nests them again after the
load.

The figure comes from the [serialization speed tutorial](tutorials/serialization_speed.html#sphx-glr-tutorials-serialization-speed-py), which runs when this
documentation is built. Download its script to measure your own machine.

[![Bar charts of the save and open times of memmap directories, consolidated files, zip archives, torch.save files, and safetensors files, for two tensordict layouts.](_images/sphx_glr_serialization_speed_002.png)](tutorials/serialization_speed.html)

Save time (single-threaded and multithreaded) and open time for each
format and layout, on the machine that built this documentation. Lower
is better. Each bar is the median of 32 runs, and the error bars show the
interquartile range. Hatched bars are multithreaded saves.

# Large datasets and storage backends

To work with a dataset that is larger than memory, or that several processes
share, create the tensordict on a storage backend.
[`from_schema()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_schema.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_schema) preallocates it on any
backend, and you then read and write it like a tensordict in memory. This
example preallocates 1,000 steps of a robot log on disk, and writes the
first four:

```
>>> import tempfile
>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> import torch
>>> from tensordict import TensorDict
>>> tmp = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
>>> root = Path(tmp.name)
>>> schema = {
... "camera": ([3, 64, 64], torch.uint8),
... "joints": ([7], torch.float32),
... "step": ([], torch.int64),
... }
>>> log = TensorDict.from_schema(
... schema, batch_size=[1_000], storage="memmap", prefix=root / "robot_log"
... )
>>> for i in range(4):
... log[i] = TensorDict(
... {
... "camera": torch.full((3, 64, 64), i, dtype=torch.uint8),
... "joints": torch.zeros(7),
... "step": i,
... },
... )
>>> log["step"][:5]
MemoryMappedTensor([0, 1, 2, 3, 0])
```

The examples on this page run in order, and share the temporary directory
`root`. To save a tensordict that is already in memory, see [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving).

## Choose a backend

| Backend | `storage=` | Result type | The data is in | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Regular tensors | `None` | [`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict) | the memory of the process | The data fits in memory. |
| Memory-mapped files | `"memmap"` | [`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict) | one file for each leaf, in a directory | The dataset is larger than RAM, and the processes that read it can open the same files (one node, or a shared file system). |
| HDF5 | `"h5"` | [`PersistentTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.html#tensordict.PersistentTensorDict) | one HDF5 file | You need one portable file that `h5py` or HDFView can open. |
| zarr | `"zarr"` | [`PersistentTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.html#tensordict.PersistentTensorDict) | a directory, a zip file, or an object store | You need chunks, compression, or an object store, or you read the data with xarray or dask. |
| Shared memory | `"shared"` | [`TensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDict.html#tensordict.TensorDict) | shared memory (RAM) of one node | Processes on one node read and write the same tensors, and the data fits in RAM. |
| Redis-compatible server | `"redis"`, `"dragonfly"` | [`TensorDictStore`](reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore) | the memory of a Redis, Dragonfly, or KeyDB server | Processes on several nodes share data, without a shared file system. |

Only the memory-mapped files, HDF5, and zarr keep the data after the
processes end. A Redis server keeps it while the server runs.

## Declare a schema with from_schema

The first argument of [`from_schema()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_schema.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_schema) maps
each key to the shape of one element and a dtype. `from_schema` puts
`batch_size` before each element shape, so the scalar `"step"` with
`batch_size=[N]` is a tensor of shape `(N,)`. Without `storage`, the
tensors are zeros in memory:

```
>>> td = TensorDict.from_schema(schema, batch_size=[100])
>>> td["camera"].shape, td["step"].shape
(torch.Size([100, 3, 64, 64]), torch.Size([100]))
```

The `storage` keyword selects the backend. The other keywords go to the
backend:

```
>>> on_disk = TensorDict.from_schema(
... schema, batch_size=[100], storage="memmap", prefix=root / "memmap_log"
... )
>>> in_h5 = TensorDict.from_schema(
... schema, batch_size=[100], storage="h5", filename=root / "log.h5"
... )
>>> in_zarr = TensorDict.from_schema(
... schema, batch_size=[100], storage="zarr", filename=root / "log.zarr"
... )
>>> shared = TensorDict.from_schema(schema, batch_size=[100], storage="shared")
>>> type(on_disk).__name__, type(in_h5).__name__, type(in_zarr).__name__
('TensorDict', 'PersistentTensorDict', 'PersistentTensorDict')
```

These are the keywords of each backend:

- `"memmap"`: `prefix`, the directory of the files. Without it, the files
are anonymous temporary files (see [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving)).
- `"h5"`: `filename`, the path of the HDF5 file.
- `"zarr"`: `filename`, the path of the store or a
`zarr.abc.store.Store`, and any argument of
[`zarr.Group.create_array()`](https://zarr.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/zarr/group/#zarr.Group.create_array) (`chunks`, `compressors`).
- `"shared"`: none.
- `"redis"` and `"dragonfly"`: `host`, `port`, `db`,
`unix_socket_path`, `prefix` (the namespace of the keys on the server),
and `td_id` (see Share data between nodes with Redis).

## Preallocate a dataset that is larger than memory

`from_schema` builds each value as `torch.zeros(()).expand(shape)`, a
view that uses no memory. The memory that the backend then uses depends on
the backend. These numbers come from one measurement with a 256 MiB
`uint8` schema:

| Backend | Peak memory of the process | Disk or server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `None` | 256 MiB | none |
| `"memmap"` | 2 MiB | sparse files: disk space is used when you write to it |
| `"h5"` | 270 MiB | 256 MiB written to the file |
| `"zarr"` | 401 MiB | empty chunks are not written |
| `"shared"` | 512 MiB | 256 MiB stays in `/dev/shm` |
| `"redis"` | 6 MiB | 256 MiB in the memory of the server |

With `"h5"` and `"zarr"`, `from_schema` writes the expanded zeros
through memory, so it needs more RAM than the dataset. With `"shared"`, it
allocates the tensors, then copies them to shared memory. For a dataset that
is larger than RAM, use `"memmap"` or `"redis"`.

To get an HDF5 file without this cost, create the datasets with `h5py`,
which writes no data. Then open the file with
[`from_h5()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_h5.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_h5). For zarr, create the arrays
with `zarr`, and open the store with
[`from_zarr()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_zarr.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_zarr):

```
>>> import h5py
>>> from tensordict import PersistentTensorDict
>>> with h5py.File(root / "large.h5", "w") as f:
... _ = f.create_dataset("image", shape=(1_000, 3, 64, 64), dtype="uint8")
>>> large = PersistentTensorDict.from_h5(root / "large.h5", mode="r+", batch_size=[1_000])
>>> large[0] = TensorDict({"image": torch.ones(3, 64, 64, dtype=torch.uint8)})
>>> large["image"][0].sum()
tensor(12288)
```

For memory-mapped files, [`memmap_like()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap_like.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.memmap_like) is
another way to preallocate. It takes a tensordict with the shapes and dtypes
of the dataset, and creates zero-filled files with the same structure,
without copying the values. Make one sample, and expand it, which does not
allocate memory:

```
>>> datum = TensorDict({"image": torch.zeros(3, 64, 64, dtype=torch.uint8), "label": 0})
>>> dataset = datum.expand(1_000).memmap_like(root / "dataset")
>>> dataset.batch_size
torch.Size([1000])
```

Make sure that the sample has the dtype that you want.
`torch.randint(255, shape)` gives `int64`, which takes 8 times the space
of `uint8`. If the path ends with `".tdz"`, `memmap_like` creates a
single-file archive instead (see [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving)). An archive cannot be
sparse: `memmap_like` writes every byte of zeros to disk.

## Read and write

You read and write a tensordict on any backend with the usual operations.
On `"h5"`, `"zarr"`, and `"redis"`, an index reads only the selected
rows. On `"memmap"`, the operating system reads only the pages of those
rows from disk, and keeps the pages that you read often in memory:

```
>>> batch = log[torch.tensor([0, 2, 3])]
>>> batch["step"]
tensor([0, 2, 3])
```

The `"memmap"` and `"shared"` backends return a locked tensordict (see
[Locking and temporary changes](concepts/keys.html#keys-locking)). Write into its tensors in place, with `td[i] = sample`,
`set_`, `update_`, or an in-place method such as `td["x"].add_(1)`. Do
not use `td["x"] += 1`: it changes the tensor, then raises a
`RuntimeError`. To add an entry, add it before you create the files:

```
>>> log["step"].add_(10)[:4]
MemoryMappedTensor([10, 11, 12, 13])
>>> log["extra"] = torch.zeros(1_000)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
RuntimeError: Cannot modify locked TensorDict. ...
```

[`PersistentTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.html#tensordict.PersistentTensorDict) and
[`TensorDictStore`](reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore) are not locked, so you can add
keys to them.

To read files without changing them, open them read-only:
`TensorDict.load_memmap(path, mode="r")` for memory-mapped files (see
[Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving)), and `PersistentTensorDict.from_h5(path, mode="r")` or
`PersistentTensorDict.from_zarr(path, mode="r")` for HDF5 and zarr.

## Share data between processes

A tensordict on the `"memmap"` or `"shared"` backend can go to other
processes on the same node, as an argument or through a queue. The process
that receives it uses the same files or the same shared memory, and sees the
writes of the other processes. [Load data and share it between processes](data_loading.html#data-loading) shows how, with
`torch.multiprocessing` and a `DataLoader`. Processes on other nodes can
open memory-mapped files on a shared file system (see [Distributed tensordicts](distributed.html#distributed)).
Without a shared file system, use a Redis server.

tensordict does not lock the files or order the writes between processes:

- Give each writer its own range of indices.
- Make the readers wait until the writers are done, for example with
[`torch.distributed.barrier()`](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.html#torch.distributed.barrier).

### Share data between nodes with Redis

[`TensorDictStore`](reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore) keeps each tensor as raw bytes on a
Redis-compatible server (Redis, Dragonfly, or KeyDB). Processes on any node
that can connect to the server share one store. It needs the `redis`
package (`pip install redis`).

Warning

Connect only to a server that you trust. Non-tensor values that JSON
cannot represent are stored with pickle, and each reader unpickles them.
Any client that can write to the server can run code in the readers.

`from_schema` preallocates the keys on the server with the `SETRANGE`
command. The server fills them with zeros, and no tensor data goes through
the process. Give the store a `td_id`, a name that the other processes use
to open it. Without one, the store gets a random UUID, which `print(td)`
shows.

The examples of this section need a Redis server on `localhost:6379`, so
they are not run when this page is tested. In this example, 64 simulations
on several nodes write their results into one store:

```
>>> results = TensorDict.from_schema(
... {"pos": ([100, 3], torch.float32), "energy": ([], torch.float32)},
... batch_size=[64],
... storage="redis",
... host="localhost",
... port=6379,
... td_id="sweep-1",
... ) 
>>> results[0] = TensorDict({"pos": torch.ones(100, 3), "energy": -1.5})
```

In another process, on any node, open the store with
[`from_store()`](reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.from_store). It reads the batch size
and the keys from the server:

```
>>> from tensordict.store import TensorDictStore
>>> other = TensorDictStore.from_store(td_id="sweep-1", host="localhost", port=6379) 
>>> other["energy"][:2] 
tensor([-1.5000, 0.0000])
```

A store caches its list of keys. Writes to existing keys are visible to all
the processes. A key that another process adds after you open the store is
not visible: reading it raises a `KeyError`. To see new keys, open the store
again, or pass `cache_metadata=False` to `from_store`. The store then
reads the list of keys from the server each time.

See [`TensorDictStore`](reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore) for the other arguments, and
[`LazyStackedTensorDictStore`](reference/generated/tensordict.store.LazyStackedTensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.LazyStackedTensorDictStore) for a stack of
tensordicts with different shapes. `LazyStackedTensorDictStore` is
experimental: its API can change in a minor release without a deprecation
cycle.

### Preallocate on Redis and fill it with a typed wrapper

A shared replay buffer on several nodes is a store that you preallocate on
the server and fill one sample at a time. A
[`TypedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TypedTensorDict.html#tensordict.TypedTensorDict) gives it a fixed set of typed fields (see
[TypedTensorDict](typed_tensordict.html#typed-tensordict-guide)):

```
>>> from torch import Tensor
>>> from tensordict import TypedTensorDict
>>> class Replay(TypedTensorDict):
... obs: Tensor
... action: Tensor
... reward: Tensor
>>> store = TensorDictStore.from_schema(
... {"obs": ([84, 84, 3], torch.uint8),
... "action": ([4], torch.float32),
... "reward": ([], torch.float32)},
... batch_size=[1_000],
... host="localhost",
... port=6379,
... ) 
>>> replay = Replay.from_tensordict(store) 
>>> replay[0] = Replay(
... obs=torch.zeros(84, 84, 3, dtype=torch.uint8),
... action=torch.ones(4),
... reward=torch.tensor(1.0),
... batch_size=[],
... ) 
>>> replay.action[0] 
tensor([1., 1., 1., 1.])
```

If the store has no keys yet, pass `check=False` to `from_tensordict`.
The first indexed write then creates each key on the server, at the size of
the batch:

```
>>> empty = TensorDictStore(batch_size=[1_000], host="localhost", port=6379) 
>>> replay = Replay.from_tensordict(empty, check=False) 
>>> replay[0] = Replay(
... obs=torch.zeros(84, 84, 3, dtype=torch.uint8),
... action=torch.ones(4),
... reward=torch.tensor(1.0),
... batch_size=[],
... ) 
>>> replay.obs.shape 
torch.Size([1000, 84, 84, 3])
```

## Non-tensor values

Each backend stores non-tensor values, such as strings (see
[Non-tensor data and unbatched entries](concepts/non_tensor.html#non-tensor-data)), in its own way:

| Backend | Stored as | A string comes back as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"memmap"` | JSON in `meta.json`, or pickle in `other.pickle` (see [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving)) | `str` |
| `"h5"` | an HDF5 string or opaque dataset | `bytes`: call `.decode()`. Starting with TensorDict 0.17, the default will change to `str` for the strings that tensordict wrote; reading one as `bytes` warns until then ([#2255](https://github.com/pytorch/tensordict/issues/2255)) |
| `"zarr"` | JSON or pickle in a `uint8` array | `str` |
| `"redis"` | a JSON string or pickle bytes | `str` |

Add the non-tensor values before you call `memmap_`. A locked
memory-mapped tensordict cannot get a new entry:

```
>>> from tensordict import NonTensorData
>>> td = TensorDict(
... {
... "features": torch.randn(4, 3),
... "label": NonTensorData("cat", batch_size=[4]),
... },
... batch_size=[4],
... )
>>> _ = td.memmap_(root / "labels")
>>> TensorDict.load_memmap(root / "labels")["label"]
'cat'
```

HDF5 returns the string as `bytes`:

```
>>> td_h5 = PersistentTensorDict(filename=root / "labels.h5", mode="w", batch_size=[4])
>>> td_h5["label"] = NonTensorData("cat", batch_size=[4])
>>> td_h5["label"]
b'cat'
```

On Redis, a value that JSON can represent goes to the server as JSON. A
value that needs pickle, such as a `set` or a `datetime.date`, goes to the
server as pickle bytes, and reads back as the same value. Each read
unpickles these bytes: see the warning in Share data between nodes with Redis.

## Backend details

### Memory-mapped files

The `"memmap"` backend stores each leaf in a `.memmap` file, through
[`MemoryMappedTensor`](reference/generated/tensordict.MemoryMappedTensor.html#tensordict.MemoryMappedTensor). [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving) describes the
directory layout, the `meta.json` files, single-file archives, and the
`mode` of `load_memmap`.

### HDF5

[`PersistentTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.html#tensordict.PersistentTensorDict) stores each tensor as an HDF5
dataset, and each nested tensordict as an HDF5 group. Open an existing file
with [`from_h5()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_h5.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_h5), or write a tensordict
that is in memory with [`from_dict()`](reference/generated/tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.html#tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.from_dict).
This example writes 500 readings of 4 sensors:

```
>>> td_mem = TensorDict({"sensors": torch.randn(500, 4)}, batch_size=[500])
>>> td_h5 = PersistentTensorDict.from_dict(td_mem, root / "data.h5")
>>> PersistentTensorDict.from_h5(root / "data.h5")["sensors"].shape
torch.Size([500, 4])
```

### zarr

With `backend="zarr"`, [`PersistentTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.html#tensordict.PersistentTensorDict) stores each
tensor as a zarr array and each nested tensordict as a zarr group. The store
can be a local directory, a `zarr.storage.ZipStore`, or any other
`zarr.abc.store.Store`. You can read and write separate chunks in parallel.
The zarr backend needs `zarr>=3.0` (`pip install "tensordict[zarr]"`).

[`to_zarr()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_zarr.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.to_zarr) writes a tensordict, and
[`from_zarr()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_zarr.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_zarr) reads it back. `to_zarr` stores
the batch size and the dimension names in the attributes of the store, so
`from_zarr` restores them. For a store written by another tool (xarray,
zarr), `from_zarr` infers the batch size:

```
>>> td_zarr = td_mem.to_zarr(root / "data.zarr")
>>> TensorDict.from_zarr(root / "data.zarr").batch_size
torch.Size([500])
```

Non-tensor values use JSON where possible and pickle otherwise. Pass
`allow_pickle=False` to `from_zarr` (or to `PersistentTensorDict`) to
reject pickled values before decoding them, or `allow_pickle=True` only
for data you trust. The current default, `None`, still reads pickle but
emits a `FutureWarning` when a pickled field is read, not when the store
is opened. Starting with TensorDict 0.17, the default will change to
`allow_pickle=False`. Tensor and JSON entries are unaffected, as is HDF5.
Unknown non-tensor encodings raise `ValueError`.

`to_zarr` and `PersistentTensorDict.from_dict(..., backend="zarr")`
create a new store and return a handle that trusts the values they just
wrote, unless you pass `allow_pickle=False`. This policy is not stored in
the zarr store: reopening with `from_zarr` uses that call's policy.
Opening an existing store in append mode does not opt into pickle.

By default, `to_zarr` writes each tensor as one chunk without compression.
To read a few rows without reading the whole array, pass `chunks`, and read
with [`get_at()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.get_at.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.get_at). To compress the chunks, pass
`compressors`. Both arguments go to [`zarr.Group.create_array()`](https://zarr.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/zarr/group/#zarr.Group.create_array):

```
>>> from zarr.codecs import ZstdCodec
>>> chunked = td_mem.to_zarr(root / "chunked.zarr", chunks=(1, 4), compressors=ZstdCodec())
>>> chunked.get_at("sensors", 3).shape
torch.Size([4])
```

zarr opens a store lazily, but it does not memory-map the arrays, so each
read copies the data. It writes one array, with its own metadata, for each
leaf, and each leaf costs one round trip to the store. In one measurement
with 2000 leaves and 100 MB of data, saving took 17.6 s with zarr and 0.33 s
with memory-mapped files, and reading took 3.7 s and 0.19 s. If you have
many small leaves, group them into larger tensors, or use memory-mapped
files.

### Shared memory

The `"shared"` backend moves each tensor to shared memory (on Linux,
`/dev/shm`) with [`share_memory_()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.share_memory_.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.share_memory_).
Processes on the same node that receive the tensordict use the same memory,
without a copy. The data does not persist. `from_schema` allocates the full
size when it creates the tensordict:

```
>>> td = TensorDict.from_schema({"state": ([4], torch.float32)}, batch_size=[1_000], storage="shared")
>>> td.is_shared(), td.is_locked
(True, True)
```

## Typed wrappers

[`TensorClass`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorClass.html#tensordict.TensorClass) and [`TypedTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.TypedTensorDict.html#tensordict.TypedTensorDict) can
wrap a tensordict on any of these backends with `from_tensordict`. Writes
through the wrapper go to the backend. [Containers on storage backends](compatibility.html#compatibility) lists what works
with each backend. Preallocate on Redis and fill it with a typed wrapper shows a typed replay buffer
on Redis.

- [Save and load tensordicts](saving.html#saving): memory-mapped directories, archives, and their on-disk
layout.
- [Load data and share it between processes](data_loading.html#data-loading): read these datasets with a `DataLoader`, and share
them between processes.
- [Distributed tensordicts](distributed.html#distributed): send tensordicts between nodes.
- The reference of [`from_schema()`](reference/generated/tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_schema.html#tensordict.TensorDictBase.from_schema),
[`PersistentTensorDict`](reference/generated/tensordict.PersistentTensorDict.html#tensordict.PersistentTensorDict),
[`TensorDictStore`](reference/generated/tensordict.store.TensorDictStore.html#tensordict.store.TensorDictStore), and

- Tutorials: [Devices and memory-mapped tensors](tutorials/tensordict_memory.html#sphx-glr-tutorials-tensordict-memory-py) and
[Storing TensorDicts in zarr](tutorials/zarr_storage.html#sphx-glr-tutorials-zarr-storage-py).
